37_marg2908: Gregory. The whirlwind is the temptation of the mind which shook the Jewish people on every side; it comes from the north, from him who says: “I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north.” For he held the mountain of the covenant when he subjected to himself the people who had received the law, and the hearts of the teachers, as the mountain of the covenant, and the great cloud. For the more he blazed against the Lord, the more he deserved to be blinded. For him whom they awaited in the law and the prophets, they denied when they saw him present. And a fire infolding: that is, by fire sometimes the Holy Spirit, sometimes malice is signified. Whence: “I am come to cast fire on the earth.” Of evil it is said: “and now fire devoureth thy adversaries.” Judea, however, wrapped itself in the fire of its own malice. All this from the north, because, led by the cold of its torpor to the darkness of ignorance, it broke out even to the malice of persecution. Whence: “I see a boiling caldron, and the face thereof from the face of the north.” But this fire burned in one place and shone in another. Whence: “brightness was about it.” While persecution is carried on in Judea, the preaching of the apostles is spread abroad in the world, according to that: “because you judge yourselves unworthy, behold we turn to the Gentiles.” Thus from the cruelty of malice that burned the mind of Judea, almighty God scattered light to the Gentiles. The fire that scattered the apostles first exercised itself in the very Redeemer of the human race. Whence it follows: “and out of the midst thereof, as it were the resemblance of amber.” By the resemblance of amber Christ, the mediator of God and men, is signified, because amber is of gold and silver. But when they are mixed, the silver grows in brightness, the gold grows pale from its own shining. So when humanity grew into the glory of majesty, the divinity tempered itself to human eyes from the power of its own brightness. Thus in Christ, as it were, while the gold grows pale the silver shines. Amber, therefore, in the fire: God and man in persecution. In the midst of it, the resemblance of amber, or of fire; for the four living creatures, that is, the evangelists, were made firm in faith by the incarnation of the Lord and afflicted by the fire of persecution.
37_marg2909: Jerome. The Septuagint: a spirit carrying off, or lifting up. Symmachus and Theodotion: a blast and spirit of tempest. The cloud is the person of Christ, who came into Egypt of this world, upon a light cloud, which is more properly said by comparison with the lesser ones, namely the prophets, apostles, and all the saints. Of whom: “thy truth reacheth even to the clouds.” And: “I will command my clouds to rain no rain upon Israel.” And elsewhere: “the cloud is the dust of his feet,” and “clouds and darkness are round about him.” The fire flashing and the brightness round about it, according to that: “our God is a consuming fire.” Whence: “I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?” Which, though it brings terror to sinners and punishments to the soul, yet glows with brightness and is full of light and splendour, therefore refining us, that it may bestow happier things on those who are pure and purged.

37_marg2916: The likeness of their faces. Some think that the four gospels are signified by the names of these living creatures: Matthew’s, who described the man, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham”; the face of the lion is Mark’s, who says: “The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord”; that of the calf refers to the gospel of Luke, who begins from the priesthood of Zacharias; that of the eagle to John, who, flying to the heights, says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,” etc. Others, who follow the foolish wisdom of the philosophers, suspect that the two hemispheres are in the two cherubim of the temple, and that we and the antipodes are men as it were lying on our backs and falling. Many, following Plato, refer the rationality of the soul, the irascibility and the concupiscence, which he calls the logikon, the thymikon and the epithymetikon, to the man, the lion and the calf: reason, thought, mind and counsel, and the same power and wisdom, they place in the citadel of the brain; but fierceness, wrath and violence in the lion, which consists in the gall; lust, wantonness and desire of all pleasures in the liver, that is, in the calf, which clings to the works of the earth. Above these and apart from these three they place a fourth, which the Greeks call synderesis, the spark of conscience, which was not extinguished even in Cain, when, as if overcome by pleasures or by fury, and deceived at times by the very semblance of reason, we feel that we sin; this they properly assign to the eagle, which does not mix itself with the three but corrects their very errors; this is the spirit that “asketh for us with unspeakable groanings.” “For what man knoweth the things of a man, but the spirit of a man that is in him?” Whence Paul: “Your whole spirit, and soul, and body, [may be preserved] blameless,” etc. Yet this conscience, as is said in Proverbs: “The wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth,” we often see cast down headlong and lose its place, when some sin without shame, to whom it is deservedly said: “Thou hast had a harlot’s forehead, thou wouldst not blush.” This four-horse chariot God rules as a charioteer, and compels it, running in ordered steps, to obey his command.
37_marg2917: There are some who think that by this the four elements are shown in one man, who is called the lesser world according to the opinion of Hippocrates: namely fire, water, air, earth; how these are mingled with one another, and, though each is joined to the others, seem to touch one another, and in one person have four kinds and shapes of living and lifeless things, is not the business of this work. The four wheels also, rising from earthly things to the heights, joined to each of the four-formed living creatures, they reckon to be either the mixture of the same elements, or the circle of the four seasons, which is made up of three months each; and the year, “turning,” is so called from the fact that it is always turning and returns into itself; whence spring, summer, autumn, winter, and month and year. And what is said, “there was a wheel in the midst of a wheel,” they think signifies year within year. Whence another poet: “and the year turns upon itself by its own tracks.” They say also that the likeness of the firmament, which is compared to crystal, is the heaven we look upon, beneath which the four living creatures revolve and pass. The throne of sapphire colour, and the man sitting above it, in human likeness, of him who by his command rules all things and has all things under his feet. Whence at the end also it is said: “This was the vision like to the glory of God”; by which, as by a kind of picture and image, they say the wisdom of God is shown. The feet straight, and the sole of the foot like the sole of a calf’s foot, or round, which signifies that all earthly things fly up to the heavenly, and, all angles being cut off, follow roundness, which is the most beautiful of all figures; the sparks glowing show that all things are full of light; the hands of a man under the wings, of the man himself as also of the lion and the calf and the eagle, so that reason, namely, sustains all things and lifts them from the ground to heaven; this we can refer both to the gospels and to all that we have set above. Others say that the four passions of joy, sickness, desire and fear, of which two are present and two future, are signified by the four living creatures. Whence Virgil: “Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.” These ought to be ruled by reason and the power of God; over these passions are set four virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, by whose judgment they are governed. Others think that the order of the camp of the twelve tribes in the wilderness is described, to the east and west and north and south, bound to one another both by charity and by blood; and that this is the wheel in the midst of a wheel, that they are led by the spirit, covered by the cloud in the desert, and lighted by the pillar of fire in the night, and do not return into Egypt but always hasten to go to the promised land. They say that the likeness of electrum is the holy of holies, and refer the face of a man to all Israel, that of the lion to the royal tribe of Juda, that of the calf to the priestly tribe, that is, Levi; outside is the eagle, namely the vengeance of God, looking on all things from heaven, which is ready to tear the sinner. Whence Osee: “As an eagle upon the house of the Lord,” that is, the temple. Over a chariot of this kind the Lord sits like a charioteer; he commands what is to be done, forbids what is to be avoided. This, as they think, is said to the people that is in Babylon, who, if it shall bow its neck to God and obey his reins, will by his help recover the land it lost.

37_marg2919: The faces: he means the beginnings of the gospels, of which the man and the lion, that is, the birth of Christ and prophecy, hold the right side. But the ox, that is, of the victims and the priesthood of the Jews, is on the left, which, abolished, passes into the spiritual priesthood, of which: “Thou art a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech.” So that all things cling to one another and are reckoned as one body. But the eagle, which is above both the birth and prophecy (which is fulfilled by the Lord’s coming) and above the priesthood that has passed away, and is outside all these, tells of the spiritual birth, how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Whence: “Who shall declare his generation?” These are, according to the Apocalypse, the four living creatures full of eyes before and behind: the first like a lion, the second like a calf, the third like a man, the fourth like a flying eagle.

37_marg2955: Gregory. In amber gold and silver are mixed, and through the silver the brightness of the gold is tempered, and through the brightness of the gold the appearance of the silver grows bright; so in our Redeemer the divinity is tempered to our eyes through the humanity, and through the divinity the human nature grows bright.
37_marg2956: Gregory. Before the incarnation the fire is within, in Judea only, and does not shine, because the Holy Spirit had filled Judea in many fathers, but it did not come to the knowledge of the Gentiles. But from the loins and downward the fire shines round about, because after the incarnation the grace of the Holy Spirit has been spread far and wide.
37_marg2957: He who sat on the throne is likened, from the loins upward, to amber, which within and without had the look of fire; from the loins downward, a fire shining round about in the circuit of morals. For the things above the loins, where sense and reason dwell, need no fire or flames, but the most precious and purest metal; but the things from the loins downward, where are intercourse and generation, where the incentives of vices are, need the purging of flames, that being purged they may have the likeness of the bow, which is commonly called the rainbow.
37_marg2958: Gregory. Through the loins the line of mortality is signified; from the loins of Abraham came the Virgin Mary, in whose womb the Son of God was incarnate. Whence: God was made known in the whole world.
37_marg2959: It is one man who, burning inwardly above the loins, held the angels to his love by his divinity; and below the loins, sending out the brightness of his fire round about, he called men back by his humanity to the desire of his holy ardour.

In the fire is the ardour of the Holy Spirit, who is also signified in the bow, in which water and fire appear; and after the coming of the mediator the power of the Holy Spirit shone forth in the human race in this: that the water of baptism washed the elect of God and the fire of divine love kindled them. For as from a mixed colour, like water and fire, a bow is set in the cloud for propitiation, when it is said: “Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.”

37_marg2961: As the appearance of the bow, etc. The bow is a witness of both judgments: the blue, indeed, in the colour of water, signifies the judgment that was made; the red, in the colour of fire, signifies the judgment yet to be made, because the world, which was first judged by the flood, will be burned by the fire of judgment.
37_marg2962: For it cannot be otherwise. Whence the poet: it draws a thousand various colours from the opposing light. This bow is a sign of clemency and of the covenant of God which he made with men, that when it appears in the cloud we may know that we shall no more perish by a flood. Whence it is clear that after punishments and tortures and the purging of sins there will be the mercy of God, but for those who have deserved to see God reigning. Whence it follows: “this was the appearance of the brightness round about,” that is, round about the throne, either of God or of all the things that were seen.

37_marg2974: Gregory. He could not otherwise have risen when it was said to him “stand upon thy feet,” because by the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot fulfil them unless he helps who commands. For it is God, says the apostle, “who worketh in us both to will and to accomplish”; whence: “Without me you can do nothing.” For it must be known that our evils are ours alone, but our good things are both almighty God’s and ours. For by inspiring he goes before us that we may will, by helping he follows after that we may not will in vain. Grace therefore goes before and good will follows, and so the gift of the Almighty becomes our merit; whence Paul: “yet not I, but the grace of God with me,” as if to say: in that I was preceded by the gift of God alone, it is not I; but in that I followed the gift with my will, it is I also. And this I say against Pelagius and Celestinus.

37_marg2981: Gregory. Whence: “They surrounded me like bees,” which have honey in the mouth and a sting in the tail. To be with the wicked in body does not harm the good, but in mind; if the spirit is lacking, the place does not help. Lot was holy in Sodom, sinned on the mountain; and in paradise the prince of our race fell; Abel cannot be made one whom Cain’s malice does not try. But let the weak avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take delight in imitating the evils which they often see and cannot correct.
37_marg2982: Jerome. They strike with a curved wound and a hollow sting, so that the same blow both opens the skin and spreads the poison; each one receives his name according to his ways. 37_marg2993: Within, because it promises invisible and heavenly things; without, because by the rightness of its precepts it arranges visible things; it commands how earthly and contemptible things are to be used or, by desire, avoided; it enjoins some things in outward actions, and what it commands outwardly is plain; other things concern hidden heavenly matters, which cannot be fully comprehended. Whence: “Stretching out the heaven like a skin, who coverest the higher rooms thereof with water.” For heaven is the Scripture, from which there shine for us both the sun of wisdom and the moon of knowledge, and from the ancient fathers the stars of examples and virtues; it is stretched out like a skin because, through its writers, what was formed by the tongue of flesh is unfolded before our eyes by the words of the teachers in exposition. By the waters, that is, the angels, of whom it is said: “Praise him, ye heavens of heavens: and let all the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.” He rules the higher parts of heaven who has disclosed to the angels alone the heights of the sacred word, which are said of the nature of the divinity or of the eternal joys, while we are still ignorant of them.

37_marg3021: The place of the glory of God is either a holy soul or an angelic spirit; and the glory of the Lord is blessed from its place when eternal praise is sung to the author of all things either by chosen men or by holy angels. 37_marg3022: And I heard. Gregory. The voice of a great commotion follows the prophet, because after the word of preaching the mourning of the penitent is heard, who before lay, as if silent, secure in their sins; whence: “He hath rested on his lees.” The psalmist begs this, saying: “Thou that sittest upon the cherubims, let the earth be moved,” and elsewhere: “Thou hast moved the earth, and hast troubled it: heal thou the breaches thereof, for it has been moved.”
37_marg3023: When we turn over in mind the past judgments of the Lord, we hear behind us the voice of a great commotion; when we meditate on future things, we are moved by those that are before.
37_marg3024: Because the Spirit of God was in him, despising earthly things he is caught up by the Spirit and hears behind him the voice of a great commotion, forgetting the things that are past and stretching himself forward to the future, so as to leave the snares of enemies behind his back. In Exodus also, when Pharao and all his army pursued Israel, the angel in the pillar of cloud left the front of the camp, and coming behind stood all night between Israel and the Egyptians, that, the adversaries being past, Israel might hear: Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.
37_marg3025: Blessed be the glory. Gregory. The hearts of sinners were the place of the evil spirit, but through penance they become the place of the glory of the Lord, and from there the blessing of the glory is heard in praise of God. Whence: first, from the injury done to the Creator through love of the world, they advance to high things even by wonderful works, that they may become living creatures of God, and by signs and by virtues and by desire fly to high things.
37_marg3026: Whence Micheas: “Behold the Lord will come forth out of his place, and he will come down upon the high places of the earth: and the mountains shall be moved under him, and the valleys shall melt like wax before the fire, and like waters that run down a steep place.” For when the Saviour came down from the Father, the high places of the earth and the mountains were moved, and the lower parts of the valleys were melted.
37_interl12400: because from the very mourning of penitents the virtues of the saints arise, so that they advance all the more in good, the more wickedly they remember they have acted
37_interl12403: because after the life of the saints came to honour, the words of the testaments appeared to men as venerable
37_interl12404: After the preaching, the first commotion is to lament the evils we have done; but after the voice of the wings and wheels, the second is with great weeping to seek the heavenly goods which we have heard.
37_marg3027: Or each living creature struck its own wings, or those of another in turn. For one of our virtues drives another to perfection, as the knowledge of the Word of God and the bowels of mercy; and all the saints in turn stir one another by their virtues to progress, by mutual examples, while each admires in another what he does not have in himself; whence: “esteeming others better than themselves.” God therefore does this in the hearts of men, as in the regions of the earth: he does not give all things to one, but one thing to one, another to another. For unless they needed one another in turn for mutual fruits, they would not have communion with one another. Thus therefore all are joined in one charity.
37_marg3028: Gregory. Because in the life of the holy fathers we learn what we ought to understand in Scripture, whose action opens to us what the page of the Testament says in their preachings: “He lifted me up and took me.” Balaam was raised up by the spirit of prophecy, by which he knew future things far off, but he was not taken up, because he did not separate his mind from earthly desires. “And I went away bitter.” The more sweet to the preacher is what he sees within, the more what he endures outwardly is turned into bitterness; whence: “In much wisdom is much indignation.” And: “He that addeth knowledge, addeth also sorrow.”
37_interl12406: to greater things, namely to those things in which the preacher advances while he carries the minds of the hearers on to the desire of God. Whence: “Fill up plentifully the streams thereof, multiply its fruits; it shall spring up and rejoice in its showers.”
37_interl12409: having understood the indignation of God and turning over in mind the meaning of the vision
37_interl12410: of man, namely; whence Isaias: “My spirit rises from the night to thee, O God.”
37_interl12411: the Son, through whom all things
37_interl12412: the prophet is not carried away in spirit but in body, which is read of Habacuc
37_interl12413: who says: “for without me you can do nothing”, of whom it is said through Moses: “I will lift up my hand to heaven.”
37_marg3029: And I went away, etc. Whither I was carried, or was borne on high by the impulse of his spirit, desiring to go where the Lord commanded.
37_marg3030: Gregory. Of Achab also it is said to the prophet: “Hast thou not seen Achab humbled before me? therefore I will not bring the evil in his days.” From this it is gathered how such bitterness in the saints, who fear to lose God, pleases God, if penance so pleased him even in a reprobate who feared to lose the present world; and how pleasing is voluntary affliction for faults in those who are pleasing, if this pleased for a time even in one who was displeasing.
37_marg3031: In bitterness, in indignation, etc. Gregory. For the book, sweet in the mouth, makes the heart’s mind bitter against itself, so that it displeases itself and pleases the Creator.
37_marg3032: that I might receive the name, namely of watchman, and teach what I have learned
37_marg3033: Gregory. For no one prevails to do this with his whole heart for love of God unless the Holy Spirit has taken up his soul. Indeed we cannot rise perfectly to good things unless the Spirit both lifts us by coming to us and strengthens us by following after.
37_interl12419: About to preach to them, he sympathizes, because speech is gladly received when it comes from one who sympathizes.
37_interl12420: seeing their wickedness and God’s just sentence against sinners
37_interl12421: that I may see first before I correct
37_interl12422: He who is to be a watchman, and is to speak God’s words to the people, ought to rest for a long time, and to grieve over what he sees, and to have none of those things in his conscience which he ought to correct in others.
37_interl12423: during which I kept silent, understand
37_marg3034: Gregory. In the prophets, as things are explained by words, so sometimes words are explained by things, so that of them not only the words but also the deeds are prophecy; whence: “I came to the captivity, to the heap of new corn,” namely the sons of Israel, whose fathers many were already dead, but of the sons more were to believe and come to the fruitfulness of good work; whence they are called a heap of corn; for good souls are the fruits of God; whence: “Israel is holy to the Lord, the first-fruits of his corn.” For the Israelites believed first; the Gentiles followed.
37_marg3035: Thesabib in Hebrew signifies the time when the new grain or barley is gathered, and after famine and want, before they are threshed on the floor, they promise some hope of food; so Israel, small and slender, as if reviving and sprung from the land of the Jewish people, promised a sowing.
37_marg3036: Jerome. Theodotion: wondering, to express the prophet’s amazement at seeing their iniquities. Aquila: resting, to show that although he was in the midst of them, he was separated in mind.
37_marg3037: Grieving, sympathizing with the wretched, as iron is first melted so that it may be joined with iron; or because the house of Israel is exasperated and does not acknowledge its fault through scourges, he sits grieving among the rejoicing, so that by his silence he shows that he had come to speak.
37_marg3038: Gregory. He had been sent to preach, and yet for seven days he kept silence in mourning, because he knows how to speak truly who has learned to be silent. For the discipline of silence is a kind of nourishment of the word. Whence: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak”; silence first, speaking afterwards. If the holy prophet, who is sent to speak, keeps silent that he may speak rightly, how great a fault it is not to keep silent, for one whom no necessity compels to speak. By keeping silence, then, let us learn to speak.
37_interl12425: as if he should not presume to speak what he has not heard. Whence: “I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my proposition on the psaltery.”
37_marg3039: Jerome. A watchman is one who always stands on high, so that he sees far ahead whatever is coming; whose life ought to be high and circumspect.
37_marg3040: He calls the preacher a watchman. For he to whom the care of others is committed is called a watchman, that he may sit on the height of the mind, and draw the meaning of his name from the virtue of his action. The watchman ought to stand on high by his life, that he may be able to profit by foresight; whence: “Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion”; that he may rise above the life of those under him, and not subject his mind to earthly things, and so see their deeds the more keenly.
37_marg3041: To speak of God is of a mind quiet, strong, and free; whence: the land up to the windows, that is, earthly care reaching even to the priests, so that, like closed windows, they cannot pour out light on their subjects, but fall silent from the office of preaching.
37_interl12430: not by death of the body, but of the soul, which by your admonition could always have lived
37_marg3042: Neither does the subject die by the fault of his superior, nor is the superior without fault, when the subject, not hearing the words of life, dies by his own fault. For death is due to the wicked man, but the way of life must be announced to him by the watchman, and his wickedness rebuked. But if he is silent, the wicked man will die in his iniquity, because the desert of his wickedness was that he was not worthy to have the watchman’s word spoken to him; yet he kills him who by keeping silence betrayed him to death.
37_marg3043: Jerome. There are two wicked men, or unjust, as the Septuagint translated: one who hears nothing from the watchman and dies in his wickedness, whose blood is required at the hands of the watchman. The other, to whom the watchman announces, and he despises it and dies by his own vice, and the watchman is free from fault. Whence we understand that the Lord therefore threatens the wicked man and says: “Thou shalt surely die,” that he may turn him from his wicked way and he may live. For the threat is not against men but against sins, nor against those who are converted from vices but those who remain in them. And it is a great danger to keep silent the words of God, whether from fear or sloth or flattery; whence Isaias: “Woe is me, because I have held my peace.”
37_marg3044: Gregory. By blood sin is signified, which is imputed to the prelate’s fault if he has been silent; whence: “Deliver me from bloods,” that is, from the sins of the flesh.
37_interl12431: He will die without you, because in the cause of death he is opposed by you; but you are joined to the death which you do not oppose.
37_marg3045: The preacher ought to announce two things: faith and conduct. Impiety pertains to unbelief, the wicked way to action. He ought therefore to strive to draw men first to the piety of faith, and afterwards to the way of action.
37_marg3046: “If any man’s work burn, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire,” so that it may be tested, namely whether the watchman is free of guilt for the death of him who perished, or is guilty. For the master’s work is the disciple’s salvation.
37_interl12432: as if he would not die at once
37_interl12433: lest he find a level way and say, “I am turned in my anguish, whilst the thorn is broken”
37_interl12434: your fault, as if he could have lived if the teacher had taught
37_interl12435: before the fall; for one had to be watchful lest he fall
37_interl12438: because you were silent, and because you were unwilling to be careful in preaching, you will be a partaker in the damnation
37_interl12439: whom you ought to have guarded
37_marg3047: As we read of two wicked men, one who did not hear and perished, the other who heard and persevered in his wickedness, so there are two just men: one who did not hear and perished, the other who heard and, being converted, saved his soul. It is also to be noted that a just man can fall, and, if he has had a teacher, be converted to better things. Good works therefore need a constant instructor, lest, having slipped, he draw back his foot from the best course.
37_marg3048: Gregory. That is, because he would not repent of that in which he had offended, God puts before the one who despises him a place where he may fall the more heavily. For a sin which is not quickly blotted out by penance is either a sin and the cause of a sin, or a sin and the punishment of a sin, or a sin at once both cause and punishment of a sin; whence Moses: “The sins of the Amorrhites are not yet at the full.” And David says: “Add thou iniquity upon their iniquity”; and another prophet: blood touched blood, that is, sin is added to sin. Paul also says: “that they may fill up their sins always.” And to John also it is said by the angel: “He that is filthy, let him be filthy still.” And here also: If he shall commit iniquity, “I will lay a stumblingblock before him.” As if, because by repenting he would not see where he has already stumbled, I, forsaking him by a just judgment, will lay before him a place where he may fall the more heavily. But this is not to drive him to sin, but not to free him from sin; as in that: “I will harden the heart of Pharao.” God is said to harden when he does not free from hardening. For he does not harden the heart of the sinner.
37_marg3049: Gregory. This is especially to be considered by us: when we commit evils, we recall past good deeds without cause, since in the committing of evils there ought to be no confidence in past good deeds.
37_interl12441: even the just man needs a teacher; whence: “to the wise and to the unwise, I am a debtor”
37_interl12446: because he sat where they sat
37_interl12447: because you had gone in to the transmigration
37_interl12449: because there, that is, in the midst of the captives, you cannot see the glory of God
37_marg3050: Gregory. The truth of the history being preserved, the divine utterances sometimes indicate causes from the place; as when Moses came down from the mountain, the law was given to the people of the Jews in the plains. And Ezechiel is commanded to go forth into the plain. Sometimes from the time, as when the Lord was preaching to the Jews it is said, “It was winter.” The Lord therefore, in the midst of the Israelites, speaking to the prophet, says: “Go forth into the plain, and there I will speak to thee”; for he first deigned to pour the grace of prophecy into Judea, and afterwards to show it in the breadth of the Gentiles.
37_marg3051: Jerome. Not into rough valleys, not into steep rocks, but into the breadth of the plain, which can receive the glory of the Lord. Whence the apostle to the Corinthians: “Be you also enlarged.” When he goes in to the captives, of whom it has been said that they are mad and persecute him, he needs a strong hand that he may be able to resist; but when he goes into the plain, the hand of the Lord is made upon him, without whose help he could not go out; but “strong” is not added, because he goes out to see the glory of the Lord, not to fight.
37_marg3052: Morally. Go forth into the plain: correct those placed outside yourself, and restrain them from iniquity. There the preacher sees the glory of God, because he perceives the glory of doctrine the more abundantly, the more he extends himself into the labor of preaching out of love of his neighbors. But from the plain he returns to the house, that in what he says he may also recognize what he himself is. For if he speaks well and does not do well, he goes out to the plain indeed by speaking, but by knowing himself he scorns to return to the house. He is shut up in the midst of the house when by the grace of the Spirit he is recalled to examine the secrets of his own mind, that his soul may rest within itself in God, and not run about through outward desires; whence: “Arise, take up thy bed, and go into thy house.” In the house, after the plain, the preacher is commanded to be shut up, that after the grace of doctrine which he ministers to his neighbors he may return to conscience and examine it more subtly, lest for what he preaches outwardly he seek praise inwardly; whence: let not strangers be partakers with thee, of whom it is said: “strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought after my soul.” Bands are put upon him, because the more he examines himself, the more he recognizes with how many infirmities of his mortality he is bound; whence: “having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ”; and David says: “that he might hear the groans of the prisoners”; and Jeremias: “he hath built round about me that I may not get out, he hath made my fetters heavy.” “He shall not go forth from the midst of them”: because on account of the hard minds of the hearers he is silent even from good things. Whence it follows: “And I will make thy tongue stick fast to the roof of thy mouth.” But sometimes the Lord, with the zeal of his love, kindles the hearts of preachers even against the tongues of those who resist, that they may not be silent; whence it is added: “But when I shall speak to thee, I will open thy mouth,” etc.
37_interl12450: at the Lord’s command he goes in and goes out, and sits with those who sit, because the captives could not hear one who stood
37_interl12451: the nations, where they were spread far and wide
37_interl12453: the very majesty appeared to the nations, which before had declared itself to the chosen of the Jews, the Spirit revealing it
37_interl12454: not bearing to endure the standing glory
37_marg3053: which he saw before, walking and lifting itself up and at times standing; for beside the river of this world, Chobar, which is interpreted “very heavy,” the glory was seen, which signifies that all the glory of this world flows past and has no stable footing. But the glory of God is seen standing and persevering when the prophet stands in the plain; it could neither stand nor be seen in the midst of the captives.
37_marg3054: Gregory. Because although man is raised by contemplation to understand sublime things, yet from the contemplation of God’s majesty he understands the weakness of his condition, and he, as it were, has no standing who sees himself to be ash and dust before the eyes of God.
37_interl12457: that he might raise up the one falling
37_interl12460: that in a good work I might stand, as it were upon my feet, from uprightness
37_marg3055: Here it is treated of the prophet in the plain, because the Holy Spirit was to be given even to the chosen of the Gentiles, who would take them up and first cast them down from the state of pride, and afterward establish them upon their feet, that is, in good works; whence: “And make straight steps with your feet.”
37_marg3056: Gregory. Historically, he gives us through the prophet an example of obedience, who now runs here, now there, and always breaks the judgement of his own will before the command of God.
37_marg3057: Gregory. The prophet goes out from the midst of the people into the plain, and from the plain returns to the house, so that the preaching which was made to Judea may go forth to the Gentiles; and when these are filled with faith, spiritual Judea may receive the gifts of spiritual doctrine which she lost before. And “shut thyself up in the midst of thy house”: because in the time of Antichrist the converted Jews will be afflicted with harsh persecutions by those Gentiles who have remained in unbelief; whence: “because it is given unto the Gentiles, and the holy city they shall tread under foot two and forty months.”
37_marg3058: Go in, etc. As if to say: because you have been strengthened by the sight of the Lord’s majesty, fear nothing, but return to your house, either for the necessities of the body, as some think, or as a sign of the siege to come; and as Isaias, barefoot and naked, announced the three years' captivity and the nakedness of the people, so you also, shut up in the house, by the very deed are a prophet of the nearby siege of Jerusalem.
37_interl12461: the darts that are foreseen wound less
37_interl12462: the evils are foretold that he is to suffer; yet in all things he is obedient
37_marg3059: And thou, O son of man. That he is shut up in the house, that he is bound, that he does not go forth, but among the multitude of captives suffers the solitude of a prison, is the judgment of the siege: Jerusalem, shut up and surrounded by the army of the Chaldeans, will allow no one to go out. This is the pot of which Jeremias speaks, and Ezechiel in what follows, in which the flesh of the people is consumed.
37_marg3060: Gregory. The prophet is bound in the house, because faithful Judea will endure the tribulation of persecution from her own kindred, pressed by the bands of sorrow; “and thou shalt not go forth from the midst of them,” because the preaching will not reach the hearts of the wicked; “and I will make thy tongue stick fast to the roof of thy mouth,” because then, the reprobate pressing upon them, the knowledge of the preachers is compelled to be silent. “But when I shall speak to thee,” etc.: because when Enoch and Elias preach, many of the Jews who had remained in unbelief will return to the knowledge of the truth. For then, as at the end, the mouth of the prophet is opened, when through the preaching of Elias and Enoch, the Jews returning to the faith, it is recognized that the prophecy was of Christ.
37_interl12463: because they are unworthy of rebuke
37_marg3061: Sometimes on account of the fault of the preacher, sometimes on account of the fault of the hearer, the word of preaching is withdrawn; sometimes on account of good hearers the word is given even to evil teachers; sometimes it is withdrawn for the sake of justifying both, sometimes for the sake of condemning both.
37_marg3062: Because the house is, as it were, of such bitterness and of such contention against God that they do not deserve to hear one rebuking them. From this it is plain that where there is a multitude of sinners, the sinners are unworthy to be corrected by the Lord.
37_interl12464: “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak”
37_interl12466: Septuagint: he who is unbelieving, let him be unbelieving
37_interl12469: from the tumult of the world
37_interl12471: is not recalled by the example of the wicked
37_marg3063: Jerome. The second edition of Aquila: he that hears shall be heard, and he that forsakes shall be forsaken. As if to say: to him who has, it shall be given; and from him who has not, even what he seems to have shall be taken away.
37_marg3064: He that heareth, let him hear. Jerome. It belongs to the same wisdom both to be silent and to speak according to the time, and to give food to fellow servants in due season; whence Isaias: “I have held my peace to a people not believing. Shall I always be silent, saith the Lord?” He therefore who was silent because of the multitude of sins, since he saw that some could be converted, of whom it is said: “he that heareth, let him hear,” etc.—with his mouth opened, speaks to the people not by his own will but by the command of the Lord.
37_interl12473: with attentive mind, considering its quality, both life and understanding
37_interl12476: the joys of the heavenly homeland
37_marg3065: Gregory. As if to say, know what you are, even if, raised above yourself, you behold divine secrets.
37_marg3066: Jerome. The wicked, though they are tolerated, suddenly fall; and the weak behold their punishments, lest they imitate their faults; whence here the desolation of Judea is added.
37_marg3067: This also is a sign of the siege. Symmachus renders “tile” more plainly as a little brick, or abacus, in whose dust they are accustomed to write grammas, that is, the lines of geometry, with a rod; whence some approve the science of geometry, observing that Jesus sent spies to describe the land, which is proper to geometry. In Zacharias also the angel has a geometer’s reed to measure Jerusalem.
37_interl12478: that is, make known to the advancing soul what temptations follow
37_interl12480: by which the city is shut in, so that no one may go out
37_interl12481: Gregory. You will bring together, that is, earthly thoughts
37_interl12482: by which the ditches are filled
37_interl12483: showing the gathered ambushes of evil spirits. For there are certain vices akin to one another.
37_marg3068: And lay siege against it, etc. Gregory: The preacher lays siege when, by the words of holy admonition, he shows to each one the virtues, or in what ways vices lie in ambush.
37_marg3069: For when Jerusalem is described in an earthly heart, presuming on the love of heavenly peace, a sharper temptation rises up; whence: “Son, when thou comest to the service of God, prepare thy soul for temptation.”
37_marg3070: The fortifications are the evils fortified coming against the mind, so that vices hide under the appearance of virtues and show themselves on high in image, though they are low in action.
37_marg3071: Gregory. By which the foundations of walls are shaken and stones are loosened. By this description is signified the city’s near captivity under King Sedecias, in whose eleventh year both he himself was taken and the city. We may, however, say that the tile is set down in mockery of Israel, because it served Pharao in clay and brick. Or the city which they thought most firm and impregnable is compared to a most fragile brick, which at the touch of water is at once dissolved; of which it is said: “Shall the hardest rock, like the mountain of the desert of the daughter of Sion, be turned into a brick,” corrupted by the Babylonian flood; whence: “therefore the Lord will bring upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, the king of the Assyrians.”
37_marg3072: For sometimes single vices strike the mind from here and there, which the preacher sets around in a circle, while he shows how smoothly lust strikes, how harshly impatience kills, and so on.
37_interl12486: the wrath of the Lord, untameable, bent by no prayers; for nothing is harder than iron; this is set up as an iron wall, so that the city is shown to be broken in a short time
37_interl12487: if the hearer will not be corrected
37_interl12489: the judgment of severity, according to that: “But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth.”
37_interl12490: you show it surrounded by snares of temptations, so that the more fearful he is, the more watchful he may live
37_marg3073: And thou take, etc. Gregory. Iron is a strong metal. In a pan food is fried; by the iron pan, therefore, is signified the strong frying of spiritual zeal, which fries the soul of the teacher, because he is greatly tormented when he sees the weak forsake eternal things and seek temporal; whence: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” So Paul burned against vices, but prepared the nourishment of virtues from his own affliction.
37_marg3074: Gregory. that if he who is taught will not hear, the teacher nevertheless, because of the zeal he shows, is not guilty, and is secure on the day of judgment. No sacrifice is greater to God than zeal for souls; whence: “The zeal of thy house hath eaten me up.” Hence it is commanded that fine flour sprinkled with oil be fried in a pan, that is, that the clean mind be burned by the ardour of holy zeal, and be mingled with the charity of mercy, which burns and shines in the sight of God.
37_marg3075: Gregory. Sometimes by acting more severely. Whence: “Hast thou daughters? have a care of their body, and shew not thy countenance gay towards them.”
37_interl12493: that is, you shall signify their captivity
37_marg3076: Jerome. Under Phacee the son of Romelia, who reigned in Israel twenty years, Phaceia the son of Manahem his lord having been struck down, Theglathphalasar king of the Assyrians took Aion and Abel, the house of Maacha, and Janoe, and Cedes and Asor and Galaad and Galilee and all the land of Nephtali, and carried them over into Assyria. After him reigned in Israel Osee the son of Ela nine years, and he was taken with all Samaria by Salmanasar king of the Assyrians, and Israel was carried away into Elam and Aher beside the river Gozan, into the cities of the Medes. In the sixth year of king Ezechias, as the history of Kings relates, Osee was taken; from which, if we reckon how many years Israel was in the distress of captivity, from the sixth year to the twenty-ninth (for Ezechias reigned the whole time, twenty-four years). Manasses succeeded him, fifty-five years. Afterwards Ammon reigned two years, then Josias thirty-two years, after him Joakim, who is also Eliakim, eleven years. Then Joachin, who is also Jechonias, who was at once led into captivity. In his place reigned Sedecias eleven years, under whom Jerusalem was taken and the temple destroyed. So from the first captivity of Israel, which was made under Phacee, to the eleventh year of Sedecias, in which the temple was laid desolate, there are one hundred and sixty-four years. From the second, when Osee was taken and all Samaria overthrown, one hundred and thirty-five years. And the years of the desolation of the temple were seventy. These added to the first captivity make two hundred and thirty-four years. For in the second year of Darius the temple was built under Zorobabel and Jesus the high priest, Aggeus and Zacharias prophesying; he reigned thirty-six years, and one being taken away, his thirty-five years are added. After him reigned Xerxes the son of Darius thirty years. After him Artabanus seven months, and Xerxes, who is also Macroceir, forty years; after him Xerxes two months and Sogdianus seven months. Darius surnamed Nothus succeeded him, who reigned nineteen years. After him reigned Artaxerxes, who is also Mennon, the son of Darius and Parysatis, forty years, who is called Assuerus by the Hebrews. Under him is told the history of Mardochai and Esther, when all the people of Israel, delivered from the danger of death, received their former liberty. And from the hundred and fifty-second year of Darius to the last year of Assuerus there are one hundred and fifty-five years and four months, which added to the former years, two hundred and thirty-four, make three hundred and eighty-nine years and four months.
37_marg3077: The left parts are assigned to Israel, which was in Samaria without the temple and the knowledge of God; the right to Juda, which was in the worship and religion of God. And it is to be noted that in the one is the punishment of sinners, in the other the exercise of virtue. That the prophet’s days are here a year is for those who suffer; and the years which the sons of Laban thought of for Jacob were as a few days. Nor is there variety only in punishments according to the diversity of merits, but also in the reward of the good: the lambs on the right, the kids on the left; whence: “The heart of the wise man is in his right hand: and the heart of the fool in his left hand.”

37_marg3079: Jerome. The sleeping on the right side, namely of forty years, is easily reckoned. For after Eliakim, who is also Joakim, his son Joachin, who is also Jechonias, reigned three months. While he reigned the servants of Nabuchodonosor went up to Jerusalem and besieged it. Meanwhile Nabuchodonosor came, and Joachin king of Juda went out to him, and his mother, and his servants, and his princes, and his eunuchs, and the king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign, and took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king’s house; and a little after he carried over all Jerusalem and all the princes and all the strong men of the army, ten thousand, and every artificer and engraver, only the poor being left. He being taken, Sedecias reigned eleven years, under whom the city was taken and the temple destroyed, whose desolation remained until the second year of Darius, that is, seventy years. In the thirtieth year of the desolation of the temple Cyrus reigned in Persia, Astyages king of the Medes having been overthrown; he, according to Isaias, sent back to Jerusalem nearly fifty thousand of the tribe of Juda, and the vessels of the temple which Nabuchodonosor had carried off, and the other things which Esdras relates. As therefore for the ten tribes we reckon three hundred and ninety years from Phacee, under whom Theglathphalasar laid waste the multitude of the Israelites, to the fortieth year of Assuerus, when the persecution of all the Jewish people was lessened; so from the first year of Jechonias, when a great part of Jerusalem was carried over into Babylon, to the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, which is the thirtieth of the desolation of the temple, forty years are reckoned, under whom the captivity of the Jews was relaxed and liberty restored to the people.

37_marg3084: The Jews, since the offence against God, eat to this day loaves baked under the ashes, mixed of wheat, barley, bean, lentil, millet and oats. For because they believe in one God, they have something of wheat; but because they deny the Son, they are fed with the barley of beasts of burden, and with beans, by which the belly is swollen and the mind is said to be oppressed, whence it is a detestable food to the Pythagoreans. For a lentil Esau lost his birthright. Millet is the food of rustics and country folk and fattened fowl. Fitches, or oats, and herbs feed the brute animals. The branch that beareth not fruit is taken away by the Father, but what is afterwards done to it by God the scripture does not say. 37_marg3279: Jerome. With the various ceremonies of the law, according to the Septuagint, by which, intent upon them, she might flee idols; these are the various garments of Joseph, whom his brothers would not have sold unless they had first stripped him; of which: “The queen stood on thy right hand, in gilded clothing; surrounded with variety”; whence: “Put on the new man,” etc.; and elsewhere: “Put ye on therefore, as the elect of God, the bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, patience”: what is more beautiful than this variety? The high priest also, when about to enter the holy of holies once a year, wore various garments. For riches do not make this variety of garments, but holiness and the diversity of virtues; otherwise Pharao and Nabuchodonosor would be written of as having had these garments, and not Joseph, a stranger and the son of a shepherd.

37_marg3280: Jerome. Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, compares the violet in the high priest’s garments to the air, in which he thinks heavenly things are signified; and one is not shod until he is washed with water; whence also the apostles, who are commanded to shake the dust from their feet, have their feet washed. And in the Canticles: “I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?” Moses also and Jesus Nave are commanded to loose their shoes, because the place on which they stand is holy; so that when the feet have been washed and they themselves purged of all filth, shod with violet, which is the colour of the air, they may walk to meet the Lord in the air, and hasten to the heavenly kingdoms.
37_marg3281: Jerome. Of which the finest threads are woven in the high priest’s garment. Of which in Proverbs: the woman makes two cloaks, namely of the present age and of the future. With fine linen the loins are girt whenever the fat incentives of lust are to be made lean; whence the apostle: “Stand therefore, having your loins girt about,” etc.; and the Lord in the gospel: “Let your loins be girt, and lamps burning in your hands.” For unless we restrain the floods of the loins we cannot have lamps in our hands. And the Lord to Job: “Gird up thy loins like a man.” Those about to eat the lamb, shod, holding a staff, standing in the truth of the gospel, and prepared for the blood of Christ, are said to have their loins girt. With this girdle mortifying the loins, Elias, and John the Baptist also, were girded; of whom: “My loins are filled with illusions.”

There is also another, spiritual, fornication, when, deserting the Church, we are joined to heretics and build our brothel “at the head of every way”; to whom it is said: “Stand ye on the ways, and see and ask for the old paths, which is the good way, and walk ye in it.” That is, in the books of Moses, Jesus, the Judges and the Kings, and also of Isaias and Jeremias and the other prophets, at all the beginnings of the ways he builds his brothel, who ill uses the testimonies of doctrine, saying: This says Isaias, this Osee, this Moses, this Daniel. And well does he set the brothel not in the middle of the ways nor at the ends of the ways, but at the beginning. For if he should come to the knowledge and depths of the books, he could not err. He makes his high place, or its base, in every street, mingling himself with the lasciviousness and vices of the heathens and the impious, even among the heretics themselves; when she has been defiled by them, she lies open, having no favour but exposed to contempt, because in easy faith she has lost chastity.

37_marg3327: According to the tropological sense, Samaria and Sodom, that is, heretics and heathens, often commit lighter sins than those who are thought to be Jerusalem, namely the churchmen; whence to the Corinthians: “It is absolutely heard that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as the like is not among the heathens,” etc. The heretics who receive only the Old Testament are wont to understand three natures in man: spiritual, animal, earthly; and they refer the spiritual to Jerusalem, the animal to Samaria, and the earthly to Sodom. 37_marg3337: Jerome. Confusion is followed by disgrace, disgrace by correction, correction by consolation, and consolation by salvation. According to that: tribulation worketh patience, patience trial, trial hope; and hope confoundeth not, in the future, namely because in the present they have destroyed their sins by confusion; whence: there is a confusion that leadeth to death, and there is a confusion that leadeth to life. And the Holy Spirit exhorts sinners thus: let all my enemies be ashamed and troubled; let them be turned back, and be ashamed very speedily; and in another place: tell thou first thy iniquities, that thou mayest be justified. And: the just man is the first accuser of himself. What wonder then if Jerusalem is provoked to confusion and disgrace, she who justified her sisters by sinning?
37_marg3338: And I will bring back. A great advance after confusion and disgrace, which she willingly accepted as brought upon her by the judgment of God. As if she said: I will bear the wrath of God, because I have sinned against him. Restoration to her ancient state is promised her. But because Sodom and Samaria were justified by comparison with her crimes, first the conversion, or captivity, of Sodom is restored, according to Aquila; second, the captivity of Samaria, according to the same; last, Jerusalem is restored. For who doubts that among the three, the Gentile, the heretic, and the churchman, he is worthy of much greater punishments who is of greater dignity? Whence Peter: the time is that judgment should begin at the house of God. And in this the prophet: begin ye at my saints; that is, that Jerusalem, last of all, her sisters having been converted and restored before, may bear her disgrace and be confounded for her sins, and console her sisters while she is more severely punished. Or let her be confounded for this reason, that she has provoked God to wrath; whence it is clear that the wrath of God is not natural to him, but that he, merciful and gentle, is provoked to wrath by our vices; whence: according to thy hardness and impenitent heart thou treasurest up to thyself wrath. And elsewhere: thou sentest thy wrath, and it consumed them. For what is joined and united in one body cannot be sent, but what is outside, as a spear, a dart, and the like.
37_marg3339: Jerome. Jerusalem, they say, will then be rebuilt, and all her daughters, namely the cities and villages and castles that had been under her power, will flourish as before, and she herself will be built up with gold and silver and precious stones; whence Isaias: “And I will restore thy judges as they were before, and thy counsellors as of old,” etc. And David: “Deal favourably, O Lord, in thy good will with Sion; that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up”; and elsewhere: the cities of Juda shall be built. Samaria also receives its ancient blessedness, the error of heretics being despised, when it is joined to Christian doctrine and faith; and then Jerusalem, that is the Church, will return to her state. According to the anagogical sense, though the interpretation may seem forced: as other living creatures are referred both to a good and to a bad sense, so also the eagle, as the lion, and it is said in a good sense: “a lion’s whelp, Juda.” In the contrary sense: “your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about.” Of the eagle in a good sense: that the just man made rich makes himself wings like an eagle, that he may be able to return to the house of his predecessor; and in Isaias: “they that hope in the Lord shall take wings as eagles.” Fittingly, then, he who had said, “I will make strength, and by the wisdom of understanding I will take away the bounds of the nations, and will plunder their strength,” etc., now under the person of the eagle comes to Libanus, which is interpreted “whiteness” and is referred to incense; he will not touch small and lowly shrubs, but the tops of the cedars, and the princes and the royal stock. Whence Habacuc: “his meats are choice.” He makes a covenant with those whom he has taken, that they bow their necks to the king of Babylon; and let the apostles fulfil that: “whom I have delivered up to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme”; and elsewhere: “whom I have delivered up to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.” We ought not, therefore, if for some sin we are cast out of the congregation of the brethren and from the house of God, to resist, but with an even mind to bear the sentence passed upon us, and to say with the prophet of the Lord: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justify my cause,” etc. It often happens that, subject to one, we pass over to another, who promises us his help and does not allow us to remain in our former judgment. But this is by every means to be avoided, lest our branches be dried up and our shoots wither, and we be thought to act against the covenant.

37_interl13403: As if to say: as it is absurd for the fathers to eat sour grapes and the children’s teeth to be set on edge, so it is unjust for the fathers to sin and the sons and grandsons to be tormented
37_marg3355: For that is a parable which is said in Exodus: “I am the Lord, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me.” And elsewhere: “visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and the children’s children, unto the third and fourth generation.” For this sounds one thing in the words and holds another in the sense. We until now think that the two testimonies set above are not a parable but set forth a plain sentence; and although we do not dare to say anything, as neither does the earthen vessel against the potter, “Why hast thou made me thus?”, yet we suffer a hidden scandal, that it seems an injustice of God that one should sin and another mourn the sins. For if he repays sins unto the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished. But he adds: “to them that hate me.” For the children are not punished because their fathers sinned, but because, like them, by a kind of inherited evil, they hate God.
37_marg3356: In Exodus it is read: “I am he who visit the sins of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation.” But here, say the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament, how great is the cruelty of the God of the law and the prophets, who extends his anger to the third and fourth generation. But these must be answered that in this too the clemency of God the Creator is shown. For it is mercy not to punish at once, but to hold back the sentence and defer vengeance. There are those who explain it thus. They say the father in us is the slight prick of the senses and the incentives of vices; the son, if the thought has conceived the sin; the grandson, if what you have thought and conceived you have completed in deed; the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, if you have not only done it but glory in the sin, according to that: “The wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth.” God therefore does not punish the first and second stings of thoughts, which the Greeks call propatheiai, without which no man can be, but only if one has resolved to do what he has thought, and refuses to correct by penance what he has done. Whence: “No man is without sin, not even if his life be but of one day.” And elsewhere: “Who shall glory that he hath a chaste heart?” And “the stars also are not pure in his sight,” and against his angels he devised something perverse. But if that sublime nature is not without sin, how much more frail man, who says with the apostle: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” He, when he has done all good things, ought to say: “I am an unprofitable servant; I have done that which I ought to do.” And that: “Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it.” To prove that the first impulse of thought, indeed the slight prompting of the mind, is not punished by God, but only if what you have conceived in the mind you carry out in deed, this from Genesis must be brought forward: Cham sinned by mocking his father’s nakedness, and the sentence was received not by himself but by Chanaan his son. “Cursed,” he says, “be Chanaan, he shall be a servant to his brethren.” For what justice is it that the father should sin and the son be punished? And that which the apostle sets on the other side, that the woman will be saved if her children continue in faith and holiness and chastity, seems not to be just, namely that if the children and grandchildren are good the parents should be saved. For many holy parents have wicked children, and many sinners have holy children. According to this sense, therefore, which we have given, it is to be understood that the sins of the fathers are punished in the branches, not in the root; let it suffice to have said this of the proverb or parable, so that the law and the prophets, that is, Exodus and Ezechiel, indeed God himself, who spoke both here and there, may not seem to differ in his sentences, or to correct here what he cursed there.

In bread all food is understood. His own: let us turn into mercy bread not acquired from robberies or usuries and another’s harm. “The redemption of a man’s soul are his riches.” Many oppress poor clients and farmers (not to mention the violence of soldiers and judges) by power, or commit thefts, so as to give a little out of much to the poor and glory in their crimes; and the deacon publicly in the churches recites the names of the offerers: so much this one offers, so much that one has promised; and they please themselves at the applause of the people, though conscience torments them; and we give the wretched occasion to rejoice in what they are given and not to mourn what is seized from them. But it is better to say that the bread of the just man is he who says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven.” Of whom we say in prayer: give us our supersubstantial or coming bread, that what we are to receive always afterwards, we may deserve to receive daily in the present age. The just man gives this bread to the hungry, namely those who hunger and thirst after justice. This bread is not to be given to those who have eaten and drunk and been filled and, grown fat, have kicked, lest they vomit it up. Whence Solomon: he will vomit it up and will defile your good words; whence the Saviour: “give not that which is holy to dogs.”

37_marg3373: Jerome. In the Hebrew, usury of every kind is forbidden. The Septuagint: he has not given his money upon usury, as in the Psalm: “He that hath not put out his money to usury.” In which only usury of money is forbidden. In the law it is said: to your brother you shall not lend upon usury; to strangers you shall lend upon usury. Note the progress. At the beginning of the law interest is taken away only from brethren; in the prophet, from all; in the gospel there is increase: you shall lend to those from whom you hope not to receive.
37_marg3374: Some think usury is only in money, but the divine Scripture takes away the surplus of every thing, so that you receive no more than you gave. In the fields they are accustomed to exact usuries of grain, wine, oil and other kinds, as though the divine word did not call this surplus; as if in winter we give ten measures that in harvest we may receive fifteen, that is, more by half. He who thinks himself most just takes a fourth part more. They are accustomed to argue and say: I gave one measure, which sown yielded ten measures; is it not just that I receive half a measure more from what is mine, when by my liberality he has nine and a half? “Be not deceived,” says Paul, “God is not mocked.” Let the merciful lender answer whether he gave to one who had or to one who had not. To one who had he ought not to have given; but he gave as to one who had not. Why then does he exact more, as from one who has? Others, when money is lent, are accustomed to receive little gifts of various kinds; but let them understand that usury is called surplus, whatever it is, if it is more than what they gave.

Yet the one who promises is not guilty of falsehood or of crime, but he who made himself unworthy of the promise. Whence we understand that they live, neither reserved for eternal punishments nor blotted out of the book of the living nor consumed before the face of the Lord. For if, because they did not enter the land of promise, they are to be believed to have perished, then Moses also perished, who only saw it and did not enter. 37_marg3476: Jerome. Tropologically. This is said of Jerusalem, but refers to the soul, which, joined to the embraces of God by virtues, afterwards committed adultery in vices and withdrew from him; and with its crimes laid bare it is stripped and disgraced and shown to all, that it may desist from its crime, and not glory in the dignity of its name, but for the conscience of evil and the remembrance of Egypt dare no longer lift its eyes to heaven. Hence its nose is cut off and its ears are cut away, because it had turned the odour of good fragrance into stench, and had heard the judgment of blood; and this we understand not only of smell and hearing but of sight also, of which, because they abused it badly, Samson and Sedecias were deprived. God also makes it deaf and dumb, lest the tongue pass on even to the earth, and all touch is taken away in those who have utterly lost life. 37_marg3495: Jerome. But note how captivity came in order from the beginning of the prophecy to the present day, on which the city began to be besieged: first the sword is called for; then two ways are set, Ammon and Jerusalem, of which the lot falls to the right on Nabuchodonosor. Silver, brass, tin, lead and iron are melted in the city. The land also is not rained upon but is overgrown with thorns. Afterwards, under the name of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, their sins are told, how the one has been taken and the other is to be taken. Last of all, in the ninth year, the tenth month, the tenth day of the month, it is shown to Ezechiel, placed in captivity, and to those who were with him and had given themselves up with king Jechonias, on what day the city began to be besieged; and the likeness of the caldron is set forth, that as flesh and bones are burned up in a caldron by the fire, so the whole city with its citizens may perish, and none of the besieged remain who is not consumed by famine, sword and pestilence, and the rest be led captive into Babylon.
37_marg3496: Jerome. There are some who according to the tropological sense transfer this place to the consummation of the world; sometimes the number which in the divine Scriptures is the number of punishments and sorrows, and which always follows justice, they temper by the mercy of the tenth month and the tenth day. For punishments are applied to the sick so that health may follow the pain. The world therefore, which “is seated in wickedness,” is set on fire with divine fire on the day of judgment, and the city of bloods is set upon the coals of fire, that what is in Isaias may be fulfilled: “Thou hast coals of fire, sit upon them, these shall be thy help.” But this is hard: how, when the flesh and bones are consumed, with which even the Pharisees are full (whence: “Woe to you scribes and Pharisees, who are like to whited sepulchres, which are full of the bones of the dead”), it should now be said that the rust and filth of the world are not consumed, but that even after the severity of the judgment wickedness remains. This is easily solved according to that of the apostle: “God hath concluded all under sin, that he may have mercy on all.” For the creature “was made subject to vanity.” And the blood that was shed is set in the open before the whole creation, that the crimes of all may lie open. But the most smooth rock is Christ, who followed the people of Israel in the wilderness, of which “they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ,” because in him all things are revealed, and that is fulfilled: “Nothing is hid that shall not be revealed.” But the Lord says that he will not have mercy, nor pass over the sins of the world, nor spare the wicked, nor be appeased, so that the ways of the wicked may perish; whence: “and the way of the wicked shall perish.”

37_marg3509: Allegorically. By the sons of Ammon, who sprang from the seed of Lot, begotten in a cave and in drunkenness by incest, we can understand all heretics, of whom John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would no doubt have remained with us.” These are sprung from declension. For this is what Lot signifies, because “they are all gone aside, they are become unprofitable together, there is none that doth good.” Against them the face of the prophet is set, or hardened, that he may crush them with his authority; and he says to them: Because you have mocked the church in persecution and in the oppression of vices, saying that the sanctuary was profaned, either by the vice of those who serve vice or by the cruelty of enemies; and the land of Israel, that is, the senses seeing God, laid waste by the choir of virtues; and the sons of Juda, that is, the true believers and those who confess rightly, led into captivity, have ceased to serve the Lord. Therefore, O every one that mocks, you shall be delivered to the children of the east, who have fallen from the light, that you also may learn to confess the Lord. But by a figure it is said that the children of the east set their folds upon them, and pitch their tents, and drink milk, and eat the fruits; and the once proud city becomes a dwelling of camels, who, having laid down the burden of sins, can enter through the eye of a needle; and the children of Ammon a fold of flocks, which are ruled by a good shepherd; that when they have been delivered to the shepherds of the east they may know that he is the Lord. And again he reproaches them that they mocked, with excess of feeling of heart, at the ruin of the people, and thought the land of Israel wholly deserted; for which they deserve the hand of an avenging God; that they who went beyond measure in mockery and joy over the ruin of the house of Juda are not delivered to the children of the east, but are for the plunder of all nations, and are slain out of the peoples, and perish, and are crushed; and they are to be believed to be not of the stock of Abraham but of all the nations; and then let them know, by the greatness of their evils, the crushing of the people, and the slaying, that he is the Lord.

37_marg3516: Allegorically. Moab, from his father Seir, hairy and rough, to this day despises the house of Juda, in which is the true confession, and thinks it as easily overthrown as the fortifications of the other cities; whence the Lord threatens that he will open or dissolve all the strength of the Moabites, so that they cease to have cities and put no trust in the art of dialectic, but all those borders, which for the dashing of the waves they call headlands, shall be destroyed; and the famous and chosen lands, Bethiesimoth, that is, house of solitude, and deserted, and Beelmeon, that is, having a fountain or above a fountain, and Cariathaim, which the Septuagint translated a maritime city, shall perish, though they have the strength of fighters, and the famous go to battle with the art of fighting and fortified on every side. Yet the famous part of their land is not a house of habitation but of solitude; but those who think they have the fountain of knowledge and a maritime city that can bear all the storms of the world, promising themselves patience and strength, shall then be turned thither, that they may be delivered to the children of the east, of the true light in Christ, as the children of Ammon, who trusted in the heretical multitude. But let us trust in the progress and in the very threat the clemency of God, that they be delivered with the children of Ammon to the children of the east for an inheritance, so that no heresy may be named among the nations, but, judgments and vengeances having been wrought on Moab for the arrogance of their doings, they may know at the end that it is the Lord who disposes all things. That by Moab is meant the pride of the philosophers, of whom: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,” etc., Amos shows thus: “For three wickednesses of Moab,” etc., as far as “because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into ashes.” For whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever belongs to earthly knowledge and is thought to be strong, this is overthrown by the art of dialectic, and like a fire is dissolved into ashes and embers, that what was thought the strongest may be proved to be nothing; whence Isaias: “We have heard of the pride of Moab, he is exceeding proud.”

37_marg3519: Jerome. He puts the sword in the hand of Israel, that Edom may be overthrown and feel the wrath and fury of the Lord, and understand that his vengeance has availed to this, that he serve the house of Juda; whence: “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.” He loves Jacob because he supplants the carnal and earthly, and deserves to receive his blessings. For first we live according to the flesh and afterwards according to the spirit; first are the vices, then the virtues by which the vices are overthrown. For the heart of man is inclined to evil from youth, and mature age condemns the errors of adolescence; whence: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember.” And it is to be noted that Jacob received the first blessing, Esau the second, and at the last it is said of him: “Thou shalt serve thy brother”; that after the flesh has been made subject to the spirit and joined to it, it may cease to be flesh, and Idumea pass over into Judea.

37_marg3642: It is asked how, after the tenth year of the preceding discourse, the twenty-seventh year is at once set down, and in what follows the tenth and the twelfth, and in the last description of the temple the twenty-fifth. But the solution is easy. Because both the earlier prophecy and this one concern Egypt, although they were made at different times, yet those which concern one province are joined to one another; which we often read in Jeremias, namely that the times are described in a preposterous order: for in some places the deeds of Sedechias are related first, and afterwards those of Joachim, who was before him. In the psalms, since the song is lyric, the order of history is not sought.
37_marg3643: In Genesis we read that on the twenty-seventh day of the second month the waters of the flood overflowed the face of the earth, and on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month they ceased, and the ark of Noe rested upon the mountains of Ararath, that is, of Armenia; whence we have it that this number is referred both to good and to evil, since in it both the wrath of God begins through the flood and clemency returns. And because among the Hebrews the month, which with us runs by kalends, nones and ides, is reckoned by the course of the moon, whence the Greek mene, that is, moon, took its name from the month. By this number it is said that on the twenty-seventh day of the moon a little light remains, lest the wrath of God be wholly without mercy. But when the whole orb of the moon is filled, then the pasch and all the chief solemnities are celebrated. In this number therefore both good and evil are contained alike: good for Nabuchodonosor, evil for the Egyptians, whose devastation is announced.

When the Tyrians saw this, and the work already finished, and the foundations of the walls shaken by the battering of the rams, they carried off in ships to the islands whatever precious things they had, so that, the city being taken, Nabuchodonosor should find nothing worthy of so great a labour. And because in this part he obeyed the will of God, after some years Egypt was given to him. And Tyre was much more cruel than Egypt.
