37_marg3672: Jerome. He returns to the order of the prophecy: after the twenty-seventh year he now sets down the eleventh, a question which is also contained in the earlier passages. For when the word of the Lord against Tyre was spoken in the eleventh year, which was set down first, in what follows he speaks to Pharao in the tenth year. And again he sets down the twenty-seventh, as we said, and now the eleventh. But, to omit other matters which are contained in the order of the psalms, such as those psalms in which David changed his countenance before Abimelech, and concerning Doeg the Edomite, and when he was found in the cave, and the fiftieth psalm of penitence, in whose title it is shown that he went in to Bethsabee the wife of Urias, these are earlier than the third psalm, in which he is noted as fleeing from the face of Absalom his son. But in the psalms the answer is easy. For it is a lyric song, in which the order of history is not sought but the songs of single deeds. In history, however, this must be said: that things said about one matter at different times ought not to be divided by reason of time but gathered together in the narration of one place; for example, that what was said of Egypt at one time and another may be known in one order of reading. When we have said this, the question still remains why in this same place the word of the Lord came first to Pharao in the tenth year, and afterwards in the twenty-seventh, and then the eleventh, when according to order the tenth should have been marked first, the eleventh second, the twentieth third, for the single prophecies. But we can answer: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God,” etc.; and elsewhere: “Who shall search out the abyss and wisdom?” We can say of them this, that in the prophets the order of history is not kept except in some places. For he does not foretell that it may come, but threatens that it may not come; nor, because God speaks, is it necessary that what he threatens be done, but he threatens so that he to whom he threatens may repent, and what was to be may not happen if the words of the Lord are despised.

37_marg3745: In the eleventh year of the reign of Sedecias, in the fifth month, Jerusalem was taken. But this prophecy was made in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth day of the month, of the captivity or transmigration, when Jechonias was taken. From this it is shown that one year and four months and five days after Jerusalem was taken, there came one citizen of Jerusalem who announced that the city had been taken and laid waste, and had come to Babylon. But one day before he came, in the evening, the hand of the Lord was upon Ezechiel, which opened his mouth, that had long been shut; and whatever he was to say, he repeated what had been done before, and was silent no longer, seeing his prophecy fulfilled in deed, and that the people who were in Babylon, or those who were captives, doubted no more of the prophetic prediction. For then the prophet’s mouth is opened when he shows by the deed what he foretold, and he cries out with full freedom when he declares things not future but present or past.
37_marg3746: Allegorically. Ezechiel is interpreted “strength of God.” But Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. 37_marg3769: Allegory. Mount Seir: it is no wonder if in this place Seir, that is, rough and hairy, is understood in a bad sense, since Elias also is called a hairy man. For Esau was red and, as it were, rough with a skin; Elias is described only as hairy. In Esau, who is bloody and blood-stained, the rough skin is compared to mortal works and is a sign of death itself. In Elias it is an increase of manliness, whose dwelling in the wilderness and austerity of life shows him not only a man but a most strong one. Moreover Jacob, who supplanted Esau and received his firstborn rights, because he dwelt simply at home and was not a hunter, while the giant Nemroth is called smooth and sleek

37_marg3788: Jerome. By the parable of the resurrection the restoration of Israel is treated. For as it seems incredible that dry bones, worn away by great age, should rise again, so does the restoration of the people of Israel, led into captivity and scattered over the whole world, seem incredible to those who do not know the power of God; yet it will come, because “I the Lord have spoken, and will do it.” Finally the earlier prophecy too, in which the ancient state is promised to the mountains of Israel, to whom it is said: “I will turn to you, and you shall be ploughed,” etc., pertains to this which is now said under a parable to the dry bones, in fulfilment of what is said in the gospel: what is impossible with men is possible with God. They were led out, moreover, from the sepulchres of captivity and from the bonds with which they were held bound in the Babylonian servitude. The Jews falsely claim that these things were fulfilled under Zorobabel, when a great commotion was made and the kingdom of the Chaldeans was transferred to the Medes and Persians, or in the presence of their Christ whom they await. But we understand it spiritually, after the cross of the Saviour, and as happening daily in those who, like Lazarus, bound with the bands of their sins, are raised at the voice of the Lord; and they are truly the house of Israel, once dry and having no hope of salvation, but, the spirit of grace entering into them and the Lord stretching out his hand from the depth of hell, they are freed; and those who had first said: Lord God, thou knowest, afterwards, being freed, will hear: O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?

37_marg3803: Jerome. The Jews and our judaizers think that Magog and Gog are Scythian nations, innumerable and savage, which stretch beyond Mount Caucasus and the Maeotian marsh, and along the Caspian Sea as far as India; and that after the thousand years' reign they are to be stirred up by the devil, to come into the land of Israel to fight against the saints, with many nations joined with them: first Mosoch, whom Josephus calls the Cappadocians; then Thubal, whom he likewise calls Iberians or Spaniards, but the Hebrews suspect to be Italians; having with them the Persians and Ethiopians and Libyans. Gomer also and Thogorma, whom they call Galatians and Phrygians; the Sabeans also and Dedan, and the Carthaginians or Tharsis. And this is what John says: “And when the thousand years shall be finished, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison, and shall go forth, and seduce the nations which are over the four quarters of the earth, Gog and Magog,” etc.; not understanding that the whole book of John, which is headed with the title of revelation, is mystical. Others, however, leaving the earthly sense and the Jewish and old wives' fables, which are harmful, and acquiescing in themselves, drag themselves down too far into the depths, ascend to the heights, and invent far worse nonsense, describing the wars of the devil and his army in the heavenly Jerusalem, and under the etymologies of the individual nations interpreting the spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places.

The inner porch is the breadth of eternal life, which now, within the narrow limits of the present life, is already beheld by the mind through hope; whence: “Go ye into his gates with praise, into his courts with hymns: and give glory to him.” For when we confess our sins with tears we enter the gate of the narrow life, but when we are brought to eternal life we enter the courts of our gate; whence: “Enter ye in at the narrow gate.” The porch, therefore, is measured with eight cubits. For there all are to be received who so order the things that revolve in seven days that through them they may reach the kingdom of heaven. For while we now act cautiously, we hasten intent upon the day of judgment, which is the eighth. Whence: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” But because no one comes to that day except him who has devoutly held the love of God and neighbour, there follows: “and the front thereof two cubits.” For as through the porch within is eternal rest, so through the front of the gate the quality of the visible life must be signified, whose measure is the love of God and neighbour, which is the scarlet twice dyed.

37_marg3895: That is, by this it is shown that at the entrance of the gate, to those entering at once, a wall of sixty cubits presents itself, with various ornaments, which refer to the constitution of the world, that from creatures the Creator may be understood. And all things running in order and reason show the variety of the world, which among the Greeks, cosmos, took its name from ornament, and was made in six days, so that for each day ten are reckoned, which number we said above to be perfect. After this, as we enter the inner court, before the porch itself of the inner gate there meet us chambers with slanting windows, which hold a space of fifty cubits, which number also is itself sacred. And after seven full weeks of feast and joy, the first day of the eighth begins, which is the day of the resurrection, and it brings us in to the nearness of the temple. For when we have done all things, doing penance for the former error, then we are made near and close to God, so that in the outer court the order of creatures may teach us the knowledge of the Creator, and constancy; and in the inner, the true jubilee, in which all our debts are forgiven us, may instruct us in true theology and bring us in to the holy of holies. It must also be noted that the inner court has many windows, not straight and equal but slanting and narrow outwardly and widening within, so that through certain small openings we may penetrate to the inner things and reach the fullness of the brightest light that dwells in the temple.

37_marg3914: The gate also that looked toward the way, etc. First. In this it is to be considered what is brought in first through the north gate; second, through the south gate; third, through the east gate. For from the north evils break out upon the inhabitants of the earth. For he who is an inhabitant of the earth, not a stranger and a sojourner, lies open to the darts of him who comes from the north, whose fiery darts are quenched by the shield of faith; and the outer court is named to the north, the inner to the south. For he says: “and he brought me into the inner court, to the south gate,” which is found written likewise of the eastern court. For the first entrance to virtue is to tread the north underfoot, and by fifty and twenty-five to reach the summit of the hundred; then to be brought in to the southern quarter and drive out the cold of the north; then to come to perfect virtue, that is, to the eastern gate, in which the sun of justice rises, through which the high priest alone enters. But it is to be noted that, though there are four quarters, of the western gate nothing is said, of which it is written: “Make a way for him who ascendeth upon the west: the Lord is his name,” that, preparing the way for the Lord alone, according to that: “Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God,” we may be able to hear what is said at the end of the psalm: “Who mounteth above the heaven of heavens, to the east.”

37_marg3928: And he measured from gate to gate a hundred cubits, etc. Gregory. Therefore from gate to gate there are a hundred cubits, so that the very delay of living, through which we grow daily in virtues, may be as it were a certain pause in going, so that the approach to the inner gate may be reached more perfectly.
37_marg3929: Gregory. And he measured from gate to gate a hundred cubits. The inner court is measured, which extends from the outer gates to the inner gate by a hundred cubits, so that he who has begun to enter by loving may have the breadth of perfection in his mind, and run through the court of perfection until he comes to the secret joys.
37_interl15604: These things, in the gate of the east and of the north, have been explained above.
37_marg3930: Through each entrance Ezechiel (whom God strengthened, for this is the meaning of his name) is led, and from the gate of the north he passes to the southern gate.
37_marg3931: It is to be noted that in the spiritual building there is an entrance to the east, and to the north, and to the south. The way lies open to the east, so that those who have well begun the sacraments of faith and have been sunk in no depth may come to eternal joys. The gate lies open to the north, so that those who, after the beginning of warmth and light, have fallen into the cold and darkness of sins may return through penance to pardon, and know what is the true joy of the inner reward. The way lies open to the south, so that those who burn with holy desire in the virtues may daily penetrate by spiritual understanding the mysteries of inner joy.
37_marg3932: Although there are four quarters of the world, only three gates are set in the outer building, which is spiritual, that is, the holy Church, by which one comes to eternal joys: faith, hope, charity. In the east is faith, by which the true light is born in the mind. To the north, hope, because a sinner, if he despairs of God’s mercy, perishes altogether; whence it is necessary that he who has been put out by his iniquity should live again through the hope of mercy. To the south, charity, because it burns with the fire of love. For at the southern gate the sun is carried up on high, because through charity the light of faith is lifted up in the love of God and neighbour. Through these three gates one comes to the inner court, that is, to the secret joys.

37_marg3934: Gregory. Above he said: the picture of palms, which is the showing of signs; now they are called graven palms, in which the demonstration of good works is signified. Whence: “That they may see your good works, and glorify your Father,” etc. Those who show that holy works are impressed upon their life bear palms graven on the forehead, because they show how great a victory will follow them hereafter in their works. Or in the gate of the east there is a picture, in the gate of the north and south a carving, because the sign of victory which is shown to beginners is held more firmly and strongly in those who return and are fervent.
37_marg3935: And graven palms, etc. Of which it was said at the gate of the northern quarter, let it suffice to have admonished this much: that what is said there according to the letter, we understand spiritually in the southern; for history and tropology run on the same lines. 37_marg3936: And he brought me in, etc. Gregory. These things are repeated in the three inner gates, which have already been said of the outer gates for a second or third time.
37_marg3937: Here again three gates are described, by which, as above, we understand preachers. But there is one Church in the preachers of the Old and New Testament. The gates above have seven steps, here eight, because they preach in concord the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit and announce the joys of eternal reward. Whence: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” The outer gates are the ancient fathers, who by the precepts of the law kept the works of the people rather than their hearts. The inner are the preachers of the Church, who by spiritual admonitions keep the hearts of the hearers. Those gates have seven steps, these eight, because in the veneration of the law the seventh day, and in the New Testament the eighth, is in the sacrament, which is the third from the passion, the eighth from the creation, which follows the seventh. But if by the name of gates we take only the apostles, who were the first preachers of the Church, who taught us to hold faith, hope and charity above all: they are the gates in these virtues, who lead us through those same virtues to the inner understanding of eternal wisdom. They are the outer gates, they are the inner: for to beginners they speak outer things, to the perfect mystical things. Whence: “I gave you milk to drink, not meat.” And elsewhere: “We speak wisdom among the perfect.” And: “I could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal.” They establish us in the first entrance of faith, hope and charity. They preach the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom to those who are advancing, and lead us by a more subtle sense to inner things; whence first their seven steps, afterwards eight, are spoken of.
37_marg3938: Each court has its own measures and orders, and there is a different grace in the same measures, while we recognize the same things in one way at the beginning, another at progress, and another at the end.
37_marg3939: Gregory. In the first description the eastern gate is before the gate of the north and of the south. In the second, between the gate of the south and the north, because Christ by his divinity preceded all things, and by his humanity came among all things, who became the end of departing Judea and the beginning of the Gentiles that followed. Above he put the gate of the north before the southern gate, because the Gentile world was before the synagogue; for Heber, from whom the Hebrews, was a Gentile.

37_marg3940: And the porch round about, twenty-five cubits in length, etc. For if we triple eight we make twenty-four, to which one is added so that twenty-five is filled up. For good hearers, who are the porches of the gates of eternal hope, hold longanimity, and the eighth day, in the faith of the Trinity, which is one God. Eight, therefore, is multiplied by three, but is made firm by the confession of one God. The porches are level, because the hearts of such are humble. They have length, because they persevere long-sufferingly in hope. The length is measured by twenty-five cubits, because they believe in the resurrection of the flesh on the eighth day through the Trinity, and that same Trinity to be one God. By the porch which is inner, the faith of the perfect can be understood; by that which looks outward, the faith of beginners. Or by the inner porch the higher precepts, by that which looks outward the least. For through the porch one goes to the steps and the gate, and through the precepts to the virtues and the entrance of heavenly grace.
37_marg3941: So that the length may take in the breadth of the former court, that is, twenty-five cubits of the outer court, and the breadth may hold five cubits; these measures, that is, twenty-five and five, we refer to the five senses, which, if we ascend to higher things, we multiply five times, and make spiritual out of carnal. Whence: “Lift up your eyes, and see the countries; for they are white already to harvest.” And: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” And: “O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet.” And: “We are the good odour of Christ unto God.” And: “Our hands have handled, of the Word of life.” And finally, not as on the north side, where they make only seven steps, but after the number seven the number eight is present, that we may pass from the synagogue to the church, from the Old Testament to the new, from earthly things to heavenly.

37_marg3942: And he brought me in, etc. Jerome. From the north side, to whose court one ascends by only seven steps, he passes to the south gate and to the court of the same gate. To this one ascends not by seven only but by eight steps, namely that we may pass through the old things to the new, that is, come through the patriarchs and prophets to the apostles, so that in the one there is a hebdomad, in the other an ogdoad. But now he comes to the highest, and brought the prophet in by the way of the inner gate, or through the court to which one goes by the eastern way. The word “way,” according to the Septuagint, is found only in this place; in the north and south side it is wholly passed over, that we may understand that only on the eastern side is that way which says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”; for through him we come to the Father; of which: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way,” who, namely, think nothing sinister about Christ, but their faith is pure, defiled by no heresy.
37_marg3943: Jerome. So that all things may be seen enclosed by the eastern light, according to that: “and there is no one that can hide himself from his heat.” But if we take the court as outer and inner, we understand thus: that God is both poured around and poured within. Whence: “who holdeth the heavens in his palm, and the earth in his fist.” And: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth my footstool,” that is, that he may be believed to be within all things. Whence: “and the mind, poured through the limbs, moves the whole mass,” etc. But when we have passed over, by the arms of justice on the right hand and on the left, through glory and ignominy, through good and evil report, through praises and reproaches, and have taken victory from this world, then palms are given us on both sides, whom neither joys have changed, nor sorrow, nor prosperity nor adversity broken. And not by seven steps as on the north side, nor by seven and eight as in the south, but by eight steps only we ascend to the heights, because the sacrament of the number eight, that is, the gospel, suffices for us, that we may say: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him so no longer,” but according to the spirit.
37_interl15621: Again, but not as above to the outer court, but the inner; whence in what follows, the porch looked to the outer court; in which the progress of one entering is shown, while in each place the names and measures are proper, and the windows round about, showing all things full of the light of knowledge.

37_marg3948: Gregory. The gates of the spiritual building have seven steps, because they preach to their hearers fear, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom. But when they command that all things now be left, and that the mind be set on the contemplation of the heavenly country and delight in its mysteries, they add the eighth step and carry them over to the inner things; whence to him who said he had kept the commandments of the law from his youth it was added: “One thing is yet wanting to thee. If thou wilt be perfect, go, sell all,” etc. By the number eight also are signified the day of the eternal judgment and the resurrection of the flesh; whence the psalm which is inscribed for the eighth begins from the dread of judgment: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation,” etc. In it all this time is ended which revolves in seven days, and that which follows after seven days is rightly called the eighth, on which our flesh also shall rise from the dust; whence by the law too circumcision is done on the eighth day, for through the member which is circumcised mortal propagation is begotten and the number of the departing and the succeeding is increased, which after the resurrection will not be, because “they shall neither marry, nor be married, but are as the angels of God in heaven”; and on the eighth day the foreskin is cut off, because there propagation of the flesh has no place, where the flesh, rising again, has the perseverance of eternity.

37_marg3950: Gregory. While the tables are described as four on each side, and the sum of the conclusion is stated, that there were eight tables on which they sacrificed, it is clear that this is not said of each of the six gates that were spoken of; for in like manner all would have not eight but forty-eight tables. Nor can it be said of one only; for after the porch of the gate is described, where two tables on this side and two tables on that side are told of, still at the outer side, which goes up to the door of the gate that goes toward the north, two tables are mentioned, and it is added: and at the other side before the porch of the gate two tables, between which the gate that looks toward the way of the north is also said to be; whence it is clear that there is one porch inside and another outside, because the inner and the outer gate of the north are both described afterwards. For when he had described three gates above, he also recorded three others of the inner court, and the outermost gate of the north. Now therefore, when two tables on this side are described in the porch of the gate, and two tables, the discourse is still woven of the same inner gate, because it is added: at the outer side which goes up to the door of the gate, and at the side before the porch of the gate two tables. The inner gate, then, is described as having two tables at the sides in the porch, and the outer gate likewise two; and four on this side and four on that are produced alike, while at each side two are described in the porch of the inner gate, and two on this side and that outside in the porch of the north gate, which together are all eight, on which sacrifice is made.
37_marg3951: And in the porch of the gate two tables. Allegorically. Our gate in the inner porch has four tables, because holy Church received four orders of rulers for the instruction of the faithful; whence he himself gave some apostles, and some prophets, other some evangelists, other some pastors and doctors, who are one order; for he truly feeds who teaches. The outer gate also has four tables: the synagogue, namely the chief priests, the ancients of the people, the scribes and the Pharisees, who were called teachers of the law. In each gate there are two tables on this side, two on that, because in the beginning holy Church had apostles and prophets, namely those who arose after the apostles; but now it has evangelists and doctors. Evangelists are those who announce the joys of the heavenly country; but the apostles and prophets have been taken away. And so these two tables were as it were on the other side.
37_marg3952: That the holocaust may be slain upon them, etc. Gregory. Rightly on the four tables of the inner gate the holocaust is sacrificed, both for sin and for trespass. For he who wholly despises the world and gives himself to God as a holocaust, here also knows perfectly how to bewail the sins of deed and of thought, either the evil that he did, or the good that he ought to have done and did not do.

37_marg3953: And at the outer side which goeth up to the door, etc. The gate also that goes toward the north has two tables on this side and two tables on that: namely the chief priests and the ancients of the people, in the greater authority of rule, and the scribes and Pharisees, who presided over the people in a lesser place. But these tables are beside the gate that goes toward the north, because, though they presided over the people, the synagogue, raging in the persecution of our Redeemer, broke out into the torpor of unbelief; yet these tables had a sacrifice, which they held according to the letter; whence they fell into torpor, who were not set on fire by the flame of the Spirit. But the tables of the inner gate have a holocaust, those in whose hearts the fire of the Spirit has blazed and burns, whether of apostles and prophets or in the mind of evangelists and doctors; which fire, because it consumes every thought in good work, kindles with the flame of the love of God all that it finds, like a holocaust, all at once. And these tables are made of square stones, because while they daily meditate the words of the sacred utterance, to offer to the Lord the holocaust of prayer, they are built as of square stones; for the words of holy Scripture are square stones, which everywhere stand firm and are nowhere reproved. For in all that they narrate of the past, in all that they preach of the future, in all that they sound spiritually, in all that they announce morally, they have a standing as on a different side, because they have no reproof. The hearts of the saints therefore are tables of God for the holocaust, built of square stones, because those who always think on the words of God slay themselves to the carnal life. Whence: “The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted.” And elsewhere: “Thy words have I hidden in my heart, that I may not sin against thee.”
37_marg3954: Gregory. Two tables on this side and on that, because in the love of God faith and life are necessary; whence: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” And elsewhere: “Faith without works is dead.” In love of neighbor, patience and kindness; whence: “Charity is patient, is kind”; that is, that it may bear evils inflicted with equanimity, and bestow its own goods kindly. The outer gate also, that is the law, has two sides, that is the spiritual fathers and the carnal people, in which there are tables: in the spiritual, doctrine and prophecy; in the carnal, circumcision and sacrifice.
37_interl15644: faith, life, teaching and prophecy in the minds of the good.
37_interl15646: when the peoples are advancing, holy preaching keeps patience and kindness, which previously among the carnal kept circumcision and sacrifice.
37_interl15648: Jerome. Namely the others, and together there are sixteen tables, by which number the mysteries of the prophets are shown, so that whatever we offer in the New Testament we may approve as foretold by their prophecy.
37_marg3955: Gregory. Because whatever faith believes, whatever life shows by example in good works, whatever patience humbly bears, whatever kindness bestows and ministers, whatever doctrine teaches wholesomely, whatever prophecy foretells, whatever circumcision outwardly left by commandment, whatever sacrifice did from the devotion of the offerer, this shows to be a victim in the eyes of almighty God. For in the law, which is the outer gate, the people also by carnal sacrifice sacrificed the devotion of their heart.
37_interl15650: because the other four are for the outer sacrifice, namely.
37_interl15651: these are living stones which roll over the earth and have with them the corner stone by which the walls of the Old and New Testaments are held together; the four, however, show the evangelical sacraments.
37_interl15652: so that they stand equally on every side.
37_interl15654: for in themselves they are perfect as far as they can be in this world.
37_interl15655: of charity as far as concerns the neighbour.
37_interl15656: because certain divine mysteries cannot be fully grasped by man in this life. For “we know in part, and we prophesy in part.”
37_interl15657: because they can neither fully know nor love God.
37_interl15658: of faith, which is of invisible things.
37_interl15659: because one God, one faith, one baptism.
37_interl15660: who take in the words of piety, so that from them a holocaust of life and of prayer is offered up.
37_interl15661: the martyrs, of whom: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”
37_interl15662: who wholly leave the world and set themselves on fire with the fire of love for the Lord, for an odour of sweetness.
37_interl15663: who still make lawful use of the world, retaining it as a part of themselves.
37_marg3956: Gregory. Because both those who in holy Church keep faith, life, patience and kindness already abound in the highest virtues, and those who in the synagogue knew doctrine and prophecy, circumcision and sacrifice, by offering some things and keeping back others, offer the victim of their devotion.
37_marg3957: Gregory. That is, to the saints, whose life stands firm in prosperity and in adversity: in prosperity it is not lifted up, in adversity it is not broken; by persuasions it is not drawn to evil; by reproaches it is not called back from good.
37_marg3958: Of the square stones. Of these square stones it is said: the bricks are fallen, that is the Jews, but we will build with square stones, that is with the apostles, martyrs and doctors of the Church; of these the porch, that is the people, has four tables built, because they take faith, life, patience and kindness from the life of the saints as an example.
37_marg3959: In length one cubit and in breadth one cubit, etc. Jerome. In length and breadth of one cubit and a half, that is, square; which, alike and joined together, make three cubits; and these three cubits have in height one cubit, that it may preserve the mysteries of the Trinity in the measure of one cubit, that is, of the divine majesty. Whence: “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.” And the name of God is as it were a cubit of one height, which embraces three properties and always consumes the holocausts of our offerings.
37_marg3960: The souls, namely, of the faithful; whence: “He is to me a vessel of election.” And elsewhere: “Be you cleansed, you that carry the vessels of the Lord”: the vessels, namely, being pastors and teachers.
37_marg3961: Gregory. The whole burnt offering. And the law indeed bids us love God and neighbour, commanded the divine commands to be kept, restrained from the coveting of other men’s goods, yet does not order all things to be given up. In the New Testament it is said: “Every one of you that doth not renounce all that he possesseth, cannot be my disciple.” And: “whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself,” etc. The tables of the inner gate therefore have the holocaust, because in the virtues of the New Testament we burn all things as it were for a holocaust when we altogether renounce worldly goods. But the tables of the outer gate have the sacrifice, not the holocaust, because the precepts of the law order tithes to be offered, not all things to be given up.
37_interl15664: that is, of those who offer up their souls to the Lord by continence and holiness of body.
37_interl15665: because for those converted from the flesh by their preaching they offer prayers to the Lord.
37_marg3962: And their borders of one handbreadth. Because through the preaching of the teachers the works of the hearers are stretched out. For in the palm the hand is stretched out, in which works are signified. In the palm the greatest finger and the least are stretched out, so that by the teacher’s admonition the hearer may so do great things as not to omit small ones.
37_marg3963: Gregory. That, from the teaching of the learned, as unity is kept in faith, so it may be kept in work, lest through the good one does, the other break out into evil of discord.
37_marg3964: Gregory. That is, that what they say with the mouth they may fulfil in deed, looking round on their conscience on every side, lest the hungry man eat their harvest; whence Solomon: “The slothful hideth his hand under his armpit, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth.” For the table of God is the preacher; he carries the holocaust and the victim, as a chariot he rules, as a charioteer. Whence: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and the driver thereof.”
37_marg3965: But upon the tables, etc. R. The names of these tables, I think, are contained in Matthew and Mark and Luke and John; their turned-back border above, inward round about the edge, surrounded them, that it might hold the holocausts within and not let them flow out anywhere, and might hold the flesh of the offering. Pardon, reader, the difficulty of the places; or if you can find something better, teach it; we gladly learn what we do not know.
37_marg3966: The synagogue had spiritual fathers in doctrine and prophecy, from whom it might draw an example of life in virtues; but the rude people, serving more by fear than by love, would not imitate the virtues which it saw, and therefore the outer gate, which goes toward the north, has no tables for the holocaust.
37_interl15666: to whom is said: “Sing ye to the Lord a new canticle”, who with the angels cry: Glory to God in the highest.
37_interl15668: one of the two, however, looked as it were towards the south and the north.
37_marg3967: Namely, behind the wall, which the Septuagint translated peribolus, which surrounded the whole temple in a square round about. The prophet was brought into the inner court, and to the north and to the south and to the east gate, and again to the north, of which it was said above. Their sense the Saviour’s testimony briefly shows: “In my Father’s house there are many mansions”; these being completed, he enters the temple, that is, the holy of holies.
37_marg3968: Without the inner gate, the chambers of the singing men. Because there are still some elect who are outside the secret joys of the inner life, who sing their desire to almighty God through the ardour of great love, and so they are both within and without. For they walk by faith, not by sight. These are the singers who do God’s commands by singing, that is, by love, not fear. Whence: “Thy justifications were the subject of my song, in the place of my pilgrimage.” And elsewhere: “Mercy and judgment I will sing to thee, O Lord.” He sings judgment who does not tremble to come to it.
37_marg3969: Without the inner gate the chambers of the singing men in the court. That is, the inner gate is holy Church. Outside this is the inner court, with regard to the following gates, namely of the north and of the south and the east. But outer with respect to the inner gate. For holy Church has two lives, one in which she labours on earth, the other in which she is rewarded in heaven. In both she offers a sacrifice: here the sacrifice of compunction, of which: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.” There the sacrifice of praise, of which: “Then shalt thou accept the sacrifice of justice, oblations and whole burnt offerings,” etc. In both sacrifices flesh is offered: here while bodies are mortified, there while they rise in glory. The inner gate therefore has its inner parts, namely that life which none of us has yet seen. It has outside the court, that is, the present life, in which every good is done that we may come to good without end.
37_marg3970: In the inner court, etc. Rabanus. Namely, it looked to the north and to the south and to the east, that the singers of the Lord, and those who are engaged in the office of angels, may always remember by what steps they have come to the heights, and diligently recognize the mysteries of the several places.
37_marg3971: Gregory. Moreover the treasuries are within the gate of the north and of the east, and they look toward the southern way, because the hearts of the saints, placed between faith and hope, look toward the southern way, who burn with the fires of holy charity.
37_marg3972: Of the gate that looketh to the north. By the gate of the north the Gentile world is signified, through which he possessed in the cold of torpor, who said: “I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north.” By the way of the south, Judea, in which the spiritual fathers burned with heavenly love. By the gate of the east, the Lord himself, of whom it is said: “Behold a man, the Orient is his name.” And: “the Orient from on high hath visited us.” The chambers of the singing men are therefore at the side of the north gate, because not only in Judea were the hearts of the saints spiritually kindled, but also among the Gentiles converted to the faith. But they received examples of this ardor from the spiritual fathers of the synagogue; whence: the chambers placed on the side of the north look toward the way of the south. It is to be noted, moreover, that the chambers are between the gate of the north and of the east, because after the incarnation of the Lord a multitude of the Gentiles came to the faith, and the hearts of the loving rise up among the faithful themselves and the sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation, which they love to the very marrow. The holy chambers therefore have on this side the gate of the north, on that side of the east, because among the very mysteries of their redemption which follow, and the carnal men whom they tolerate within holy Church, many of the Jews advance by strong love; and among those things which they love and those which they tolerate, like certain chambers they keep the riches of the spirit in the mind, and do not fail among these things, but stretch the eyes of the mind toward the southern way. For what do we suffer that our fathers did not endure for the love of God? The eastern gate is described as between the gate of the south and of the north, because the Lord, born of Judea, soon drew the Church from the Gentiles into his faith. The eastern gate also looks to the gate of the north, because the Lord forsook the synagogue and gathered the multitude of the Gentiles.
37_marg3973: Against the way, that is, there is one way for all, which says: “I am the way.”
37_marg3974: Gregory. Because after sins forgiven in baptism, and after faith received, we all offend in many things; therefore let us lift the eyes of the mind to the way of the south, so that, burning with holy charity, the heat of love may free us from the fault of sluggishness and coldness.

37_marg3977: Of the just, or of the justifying, that is, of almighty God, of whom: “The Lord is just, and hath loved justice: his countenance hath beheld righteousness.”
37_marg3978: Jerome. Levi is interpreted “taken up”; and they are taken up by the Lord that they may come near to him, lest it be said of Moses alone: “Moses drew near to the Lord,” but that all who minister to God may be said to draw near.
37_marg3979: Of the sons of Levi: Of these sons it is said: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God.”
37_interl15689: the same who brought me in, that is, into the inner court, that is, the holy of holies
37_interl15690: the breadth of the faithful peoples
37_interl15694: that the priests of the Lord, serving in ministry, who had entered by the narrow and strait way, may have the broadest walking places, and may dwell in the perfect and complete number of virtues
37_interl15695: that the life of the faithful may be equally perfected in the four virtues: namely justice, fortitude, temperance and prudence
37_interl15696: the greater: a living victim, holy and pleasing to God
37_interl15697: to be looked upon as an example
37_interl15698: of the lesser, who nonetheless are the temple of God
37_marg3980: The court itself, in which were two exedrae or treasuries, assigned as dwellings for the guardians of the temple or of the altar.
37_marg3981: A hundred cubits in length and in breadth, etc. Gregory. The length of hope and the breadth of charity are not void in the hearts of the faithful, for through faith they work whatever they can. For “in Christ Jesus only faith availeth, which worketh by charity.” If therefore in the life of the faithful, each according to his measure, the longanimity of hope and the breadth of charity and the certainty of faith and the zeal of work are perfect, the court of the temple has a hundred cubits foursquare, in which all the sides are equal; for while we live in this life we find all these virtues equal in us. For as much as we love, so much we presume from hope, and as much as we believe, so much we love. But of faith and work John says: “He who saith that he knoweth God, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar.” For the knowledge of God pertains to faith, the keeping of the commandments to work. Yet charity is called greater than faith and hope, because when in the future those shall cease, this shall be perfected.
37_marg3982: That is, it was in the court itself, so that the prayer of the saints to the Lord may never cease.
37_interl15699: because he who had entered was instructed in divine senses, and went in neither to the right nor to the left, but by the royal way
37_interl15700: by which one enters into the porch of the temple
37_interl15701: the mystery of the Trinity, which is the gate to the Lord, since the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. This number is the one gate of those who, after baptism, come to salvation through the Trinity
37_marg3983: Jerome. It is elegantly said, not on the right nor on the left, lest there should seem to be anything left-handed in the holy of holies.
37_interl15702: that is, by the sacred number
37_interl15704: Whence: “He that shall overcome, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.”
37_interl15705: Peter and John are called pillars of the Church
37_interl15706: He does not say two, lest a dual number occur, but one and one, which is a perfect number.
37_interl15707: This number is taken for the unity of God.
37_marg3984: The number twenty, like the dual, because of the two tens, is wont to be taken in a bad sense, as is eleven, which lacks one to fill the sacred number, namely twelve; and yet they are said to be in the porch of the temple, because although the priests are holy and placed in the ministries of the temple and offer victims daily to Christ, yet because they dwell in a frail body subject to vices, they have twenty and eleven. Whence: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”
37_marg3985: The holy pillars of the Church: Peter and John, two pillars through whom we enter into the holy of holies, and by whose teaching our entrance is to Christ.
37_interl15708: At length, after many mysteries and various entrances, and in individual places their properties.
37_marg3986: Isidore. The sacrament of all creatures. For the world was made in six days; through knowledge of these, and of the causes and reason of their making, we enter into the temple of God, and from the order and constancy of creatures we know the Creator.
37_interl15709: Which is a sacred and perfect number, in which, in the seventh month on the tenth day of the month, is the fast of atonement.
37_interl15710: Or shoulders. Whence: “I put my shoulder to work.” Also in the high priest’s vestment the shoulder-piece is bound with the breastplate, so that works may be completed by reason. Whence: “By thy commandments I have had understanding.”
37_interl15711: Of the gate, of whose breadth and shoulders he has spoken only above.
37_marg3987: Of ten cubits. Jerome. On the tenth day of the first month, which is called Nisan, the lamb is taken for the immolation and preparation of the pasch. In the seventh month, then, the tenths are offered into the barns of God, or, as Scripture is wont to say, the winepresses. Whence: be enlarged you also; so that when anyone has entered the temple through the ten cubits of the gate, the sides on both parts of it, or, as is properly said in the Hebrew, the shoulders, which refer to works, are measured. These shoulders of the gate on both sides have five cubits each, so that through the earthly and divine senses, of whose difference it was said above, they may enter the approaches of the temple.
37_marg3988: Twenty times forty makes eight hundred, which number is near to eight. Whence: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” Or because through the tribulations and straits of this world we enter into the sanctuary of God. For forty is the number of labor. Whence: Moses and Elias fast by this number, and Israel is vexed and tried in the wilderness, and after many labors enters the land of promise. And our Lord, according to the frailty of the body he assumed, is tempted forty days in the wilderness, that after the victory the angels may come and minister to him.
37_marg3989: And twenty cubits in breadth. When after tribulations and straits we shall say with the apostles: “in all things we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed.” And with the prophet: “in tribulation thou hast enlarged me.” Then may the widest entrance be opened to us, which has a breadth of twenty cubits. This too is a dual number, that having overcome the struggles of the world and of earthly things they may enter the inmost parts of the temple, and we may hear with the disciples: “Have confidence, I have overcome the world.”
37_interl15712: Although we always advance, a greater progress is opened to us; whence, after entering the temple, he enters again inwardly.
37_marg3990: According to the higher sense, through the dual number we enter to the place where the holy of holies is. Whence: “and the gate six cubits”, through which, having entered, we possess eternal rest, which is shown in the sevenfold number.
37_marg3991: Because before the face of the temple, and at its very entrance, the measure of our past labour and struggle always meets us; for whatever reason the double holds in the single numbers, two tens have the same.
37_marg3992: Jerome. Note that in the description of the tabernacle the holies of holies are spoken of in the plural, but here the holy of holies in the singular, that after the holies we may come to the holy, as after many songs to the Song of Songs, which is the song of all songs, which singing we are joined to the bridegroom and embrace him.
37_marg3993: If the holy of holies is before the face of the temple, how great a blessedness must we judge to be in the inner parts of the temple? Whence: “This labour is before me, until I go into the sanctuary of God, and understand concerning their last ends.”
37_interl15714: For the structure of the world and every visible creature that was made in six days.
37_marg3994: Isidore. These four show the elements from which all things are compacted, and especially human bodies; fighting against these, and subjecting them to the power of the soul, the holy deserve to enter the inner parts and to know the secrets of the Lord.
37_marg3995: And the side chambers, etc. Rabanus. The side chambers themselves, which were round about the house and were separated by four cubits from the wall of the temple, were joined to one another, so that one side chamber touched another, and had in length not thirty-three cubits but twice thirty-three, that is, sixty-six. In Leviticus it is said: at the birth of a male, after one week, both the woman who bore and the one who was born are to fulfil thirty-three days, that they may come to purification. But if she bear a female, they are to observe a double number, that is, sixty-six. And because to come to the holies of holies we need not only the first birth but also the second, that born in the flesh we may be born again in the spirit, therefore not sixty-six but twice thirty-three are set down, that each birth may be owed to God the author and to his elements, and that the side chambers which support the structure of the temple may go round the house in a double circuit.
37_marg3996: And there were projections, etc. For holy men break forth through the wall of the temple in the multitude of believers: namely through all the sides round about; and they hold up the foundations of the church, and yet they do not touch the wall of the temple, content only to have seen, and from afar to have adored the unspeakable mysteries; for we see now through a glass in a dark manner, and we cannot touch and comprehend in the fullest truth.
37_marg3997: Isidore. This most beautiful figure is found even among the philosophers: the heaven, the sun, the moon and the other stars, and the point of the earth; and in human bodies the eyes, like other stars, and the shape of the head, which is the receptacle of all the senses; the rounded fingers and thighs and arms are marked by this roundness.
37_marg3998: The things that are below are always narrower, in fasting and in the restraint of a single diet; and little by little, as we climb to the heights, a broader way opens to us; whence: “Thou hast enlarged me when I was in distress.”
37_marg3999: Rabanus. In the book of Kings, Eliseus and Elias had this upper room. And in the Acts of the Apostles: Tabitha, that is, Dorcas, and our Damula, who by good works had ascended to the heights. Peter also, upon whom the Lord set the foundations of the church, went up beyond the upper room and came to the roof, which in Greek is doma, that is, the sun-terrace of the roof, and learned the sacraments of the Church, unknown before to the world. The Saviour also, in a large and broad upper room, cleansed of all filth, furnished and prepared for a spiritual banquet, made the pasch, delivered to his disciples the mystery of his body and blood, and left us the eternal festival of the spotless Lamb.
37_marg4000: By these it is signified that from this world and from earthly senses, and from the dual number of two decades, which amounts to twenty, we deserve to ascend not only into the holy of holies but also into their upper rooms, and always to keep in memory that through the six days of our creation, and through the five senses, and through the twenty cubits of breadth, we have ascended to the upper room of the temple, and leaving earthly lowliness and the sense of the letter, we have passed over to the summit of the church, and rejoice in the fellowship of the Spirit.
37_interl15718: From which evils blaze out upon the earth.
37_marg4001: Fittingly the place of prayer is at the door toward the north, that according to the apostle we may pray without ceasing and say with Jeremias: let not the apple of my eye cease, whether desiring to avoid present evils or giving thanks for things past. For in the tabernacle of this body we always groan and say: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”
37_marg4002: Jerome. For after the cold of the north we pass to the heat of the south; and yet again the place of prayer is within: at the door of the north, that we may escape dangers; in the south, that we may give thanks for things past, and the possession of victory may be secure for us. The five cubits also in this place indicate the divine senses, by which we ascend from earthly things to higher.
37_marg4003: That is, that after labours and dangers, and the waves and shipwrecks of this world, of which Jeremias writes, and Daniel and Zacharias, we may attain the true and lawful sabbath of seven decades, and eternal rest may be ours. And through the breadth of five cubits we come to the length of ninety cubits. At which age Sara, by the promise, bore a son, who at ninety years, that is, nine decades, brought forth Isaac, joined to Abraham, a hundred years old, that is, ten decades, who has the mystery. What this number signifies the following Scripture will show.
37_marg4004: Jerome. This number is perfect, ten tens, that we may serve the Lord in mind, word and deeds, remembering that saying of the apostle: “that you may be able to comprehend what is the breadth, and length, and height, and depth.”
37_marg4005: Ecthetae, which they call solaria at Rome, projections from the walls of upper rooms, or maeniana from their inventor, which some of the Greeks call exostrae.
37_interl15723: Of wisdom and life, which is in paradise.
37_interl15724: Until that which is perfect comes.
37_marg4006: Jerome. Pardon, reader, the difficulty, and grant forgiveness to one who confesses it; for we look through oblique windows, made in the manner of a net, and always closed, and we can scarcely send the eye as far as the inner house of our heart, so that all things we perceive we see in shadow and image, that we may cry out with the apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!” etc. Who has known the mind of the Lord, except the angel of great counsel, who, being worthy, can open his mysteries?
37_marg4007: Which they call solaria at Rome, projections from the walls of upper rooms, or maeniana from their inventor, which some of the Greeks call exostrae.
37_interl15725: For nothing in the temple of God is without measure and reason.
37_interl15726: that is, in the wood, which reached from the pavement up to the windows
37_interl15730: so that one was fenced in by the sides of two palm trees
37_interl15731: not four, as above, namely of man, lion, calf and eagle
37_interl15733: in which is anger, which in Greek is more significantly called thymos; not that which is disturbance and next to vice, but that which strengthens the softness of the mind and makes the spirit of one fighting braver
37_marg4008: The face of a man by the palm tree, etc. Rabanus. In the beginning we are subject to concupiscence, which is referred to the calf because of earthly works. And some things are carnal, others spiritual, the last of which is assigned to the eagle. But when we have entered the holy of holies and possessed the inner parts of the temple, we need nothing but reason and fortitude, of which the one is referred to understanding and foresight, the other to perseverance of soul. Every wall, therefore, round about the temple, from the pavement up to the ceilings, had cherubim and palm trees wrought with wonderful art. After these the sanctuary was opened through four corners, facing the face of the holy things. For first we have a multitude of knowledge, through which we win victory over the enemy, and afterwards the sanctuary is opened to us, and the temple, which has four corners, that is, a most firm standing that inclines to no side. For a square is made firm on a stable base, and in the mystical number four signifies the four elements, of which all solid and lasting things consist. And all things looked toward the face of the sanctuary, before which sanctuary was the appearance of an altar of wood.

37_marg4038: First he measured toward the eastern quarter five hundred reeds round about. This wall had together two thousand reeds. But if a reed was of six cubits and of the sixth part of a cubit, it is plain that the outer wall had round about two thousand reeds, which make twelve thousand three hundred thirty-three cubits and a third, from the two thousand reeds. In the Book of Jesus Nave, in the suburbs, this measure is carefully kept. The legion of devils also chose this number for the drowning of the swine, so that what was separated by the precept of the Lord from those who serve God might be referred to the opposite side, to the perdition of those who lead a life worthy of filth and foulness. Every wall that is outer and has a spacious length and breadth foursquare contains the number of the apostles, that is, twelve thousand, so that a thousand is reckoned to each apostle, and yet it does not come to the measure of the fulness of Christ and of the perfect man unless there be joined to it also the palm-breadth, which makes three hundred thirty-three cubits and a third part of a cubit, through which the mystery of the Trinity is shown, which girds and fortifies all things and renders the dwellers in its temple most safe. Whence the ark of Noe has a length of three hundred cubits and a height of thirty cubits, which is finished in one cubit. But that fifty cubits are added there in breadth is a sacrament of remission. Whence also the Lord came at thirty years to baptism, and Ezechiel at the beginning of the volume sets the thirtieth year, and the three hundred thirty-third number is completed by three added and a third part. But as for what the Septuagint have, and the Latin translation, while in the speed of dictating we look less carefully, namely “the wall of it round about, a length of five hundred cubits,” the Hebrew truth does not have this, but simply a length of five hundred, and the Latin of five hundred, so that “reeds” is understood.

37_marg4059: Rabanus. From the lesser propitiatory, etc. The lesser propitiatory is the stone cut out of the mountain without hands. The great propitiatory is the same stone which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth. Or the lesser propitiatory is when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; the great propitiatory, when he received the glory which he had with the Father before the world was made; for we first acknowledge the lowly things of Christ, and so come to the height of the divinity. And the propitiatory of both natures belongs only to the sacrament of the one altar. Between the two propitiatories are four cubits, signifying the four elements of the world, which themselves also come to the breadth of one cubit. And it is to be noted that in the measure of the altar the first cubit in breadth is joined to none, but is perfect by its own unity. But the second cubit of breadth, after two cubits, grows to the top. And the third, after the lesser and the greater propitiatory, through the four elements tends to the mystery of one cubit, so that the first and second and third cubit in the altar of the Lord are said to be not first, second and third, but one and one and one.

37_marg4071: After the altar and its measures were shown on the top of the mountain, and the consecration and expiation through one calf without blemish and a he-goat, or, according to the Septuagint, two kids, of which the calf pertains to Christ, and the others to the apostles and ministers, lest in the consecration of the spiritual altar, which properly pertains to the Church, the law and the prophets should seem to be excluded. Therefore, the altar being consecrated, a calf without blemish and a ram are taken up and are offered in the sight of the Lord. And the sons of Sadoch, that is, the priests of the just, sprinkle salt upon their heads, that the law, namely, and the prophets may be seasoned with the savour of the gospel; nor is there any sacrifice, according to the command of the law and the apostle (who says: “let your speech be seasoned with salt”), that lacks salt. And each is offered as a holocaust to the Lord, that the body, which is signified in the law, and the cloudiness of prophecy, may be converted by the fire of the Lord, that is, the Holy Spirit (of whom it is said, “fervent in spirit”), into a spiritual and subtle substance.
37_marg4072: That by these sacrifices the altar is cleansed to perfection over seven days. In the seven is signified the sabbath rest that is kept for the people of God, in which we hope for true rest, and do not do the servile work of sin.
37_marg4073: In the he-goat and the calf and the ram are shown the three general sins to which the human race is subject. For we sin either by thought, or by word, or by deed. Thought pertains to the ram; it is the first of all sins, and from it two kinds are born. The kid and the he-goat pertain to speech, which disputes about higher things. Works are signified in the calf, which is made subject to the plough and to labour and to earthly works. These, therefore, we ought to offer to God without blemish through the seven days of the true and perfect sabbath, and to expiate the altar, that our prayer may come clean to God.
37_marg4074: By the gifts of the sacrifice, namely for the high priest, for the priests, and for the people, so that no one stands empty before the Lord.
37_marg4075: That they may say with the apostle: “we are risen with Christ,” and may reach beyond the eighth day to heavenly things, and offer for us a holocaust, or the things that are for the peace of our sins and our salvation, that through the fire of the Holy Spirit all that we think, speak and do may be converted into spiritual substance.

37_marg4078: THIS GATE WAS SHUT, etc. Rabanus. Before the Saviour took on a human body and, taking the form of a servant, humbled himself, the law and the prophecy and all knowledge of the Scriptures were shut; paradise was closed.
37_marg4079: But after he hung on the cross and said to the thief, “this day thou shalt be with me in paradise,” at once the veil of the temple was rent and all things were opened, and the veil being taken away we say: “but we all beholding the glory of the Lord with open face,” etc. If all things have been revealed in Christ, how will the gate be shut and not be opened? But although we have come to the highest knowledge, in comparison with divine knowledge “we know in part,” “we know in part”; “but when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away.” Whence Paul too calls himself now perfect, now imperfect. For he is perfect in comparison with others, imperfect in comparison with divine knowledge.
37_marg4080: But that the eastern gate beyond the bounds of the world is always shut, John makes known when he says: “No man hath seen God at any time: the only begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.” As if he had said in other words: “And it shall be shut for the prince, and the prince himself shall sit in it” to eat bread of perfect and consummate knowledge. “But no one knoweth the Son but the Father, and no one knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him.”

37_marg4090: But the Levites also who went far away, etc. Jerome. According to the Septuagint it means that the Levites of the priestly rank who went astray, after they have received their iniquities, shall stand in the sanctuary and slay the holocausts, and these shall stand to minister to them, etc. But if so, how can it stand that Levites who departed after idols should themselves minister in the house and slay the holocausts? For what more will the priests, the sons of Sadoch, do, who kept the ceremonies of God? The Hebrew has this sense: the wicked Levites shall bear their iniquities, because they were ministering in my sanctuary in the office of the gates. For they themselves offered the holocausts and victims and stood in the sight of the Lord, etc. Symmachus, considering the order of the reading and the sense, interprets more rightly, saying: I had set them as keepers of the doors of the house, and of all its ministry, and of all that is done in it, so that it does not pertain to those who are to be in the temple but to those who were.

37_marg4094: With linen garments, that is, when this mortal shall put on immortality, and this corruptible, incorruption. These garments we make for ourselves by our own labour; those that are woven from above, such as the tunic the Lord had, which could not be torn, we put on when we know the secret and hidden things of the Lord, and have the Spirit, who searcheth even the deep and profound things, which are not to be shown to the people who are not sanctified nor prepared for the holiness of the Lord, lest, if they should hear things greater than themselves, they be unable to bear the majesty of knowledge, and be choked as it were by solid food, who must still be nourished with milk. There are also the worst garments. Whence: “He put on cursing, like a garment.” And a little after: “May it be unto him like a garment which covereth him; and like a girdle with which he is girded continually.” Whence also the Lord, who bore our sins, is said in Zacharias to have filthy garments.

37_marg4097: And when they shall go forth to the outward court to the people, etc. Rabanus. It is a grave thing to take on the burden of a multitude beyond one’s strength, as Solomon says: “It is a snare for a man quickly to sanctify something of his own”; for when he has made a vow, repentance creeps in. The Nazarites offer themselves of their own will, and whoever has vowed anything and not fulfilled it is guilty of the vow. Whence of the widows: “Having damnation, because they have made void their first faith.” It is better not to promise than not to perform what is promised. Anna offered Samuel, who remained in eternal holiness. Manue offered his son Samson, but the lust of Dalila troubled the sanctification of his hair, and the Lord departed from him, and he was condemned to blindness; except that afterwards, as his hair grew, he received his former strength, and, in the type of Christ, he fell having slain many more of the foreigners in death than in life.
37_marg4098: Rabanus. Lest, if they have holy garments, they sanctify the people who stand outside, who have not yet been sanctified nor prepared themselves in the sanctification of the temple, so as to be a Nazarite of the Lord. Whence: we learn that we ought not to enter the holy of holies in everyday garments, defiled by the common use of life, but with a clean conscience and clean garments to hold the sacraments of the Lord.
37_interl15913: The hairs of the apostles’ heads are all numbered. Of this head it is said: “The eyes of a wise man are in his head”; and the head of the man is Christ.
37_interl15914: So that they are not with shaven heads, as is the custom for priests and worshippers of Isis and Serapis; nor again let them let their hair grow, which properly belongs to the lustful, to barbarians and to soldiers; but let the dress of the priests be honourable.
37_marg4099: But they shall not shave their head. Rabanus. The Lord wills that his priests have the hair of sanctification perpetual, and that their heads be covered not by any covering from outside but by their own natural hair, not for ornament and luxury but for decency. Whence: “the very hairs of your head are all numbered.” Of which head it is read: “the eyes of a wise man are in his head”; the head of man is Christ, which the sinner tramples upon and despises, and shaves with a razor and takes away its beauty. This the sons of Ammon also did to those whom David had sent as ambassadors. But if the transgressor of the law dishonours God, he who keeps the precepts of the king honours him, “that all men may honour the Son, as they honour” the Father.
37_marg4100: Shall not shave. Pagan superstition has shaven heads.
37_interl15915: In which there is luxury; of which: “It is good not to drink wine and not to eat flesh.” “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” The apostle allows wine to Timothy, but because of infirmity.
37_marg4101: Because by drunkenness the steadiness of the mind is overturned, which is understood of all vices and of all worldly business, by which the mind is made drunk and wavers and cannot hold steady. And because we are surrounded with frail flesh and are compelled, for food, drink, clothing and the necessities of the body, to do what we ought not, this at least is required of us: that when we return to ourselves and know why we were born and enter the inner parts of the temple, we depart from vices and commit not even the least sins; by which it is shown both that we sin for the needs of the flesh, with light sins, and again that there is a time when, entering the court beyond, we ought to be altogether free of all the drunkenness of the world.

37_interl15926: Not of those of whom it is said: “Your new moons and your sabbaths my soul hateth.” And elsewhere: “The priests in the temple break the sabbath, and are without blame”: the sabbath, namely, of the Jews, which they rightly break who are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood.

37_marg4103: Rabanus. The first virtue of a priest is not only to teach what he knows but to keep all the festivals of God, that he may be able to command others to keep them, since he himself is zealous to observe them. And it is the priest’s office to have knowledge of the law. Whence Malachias: “the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge,” etc.
37_marg4104: Rabanus. Namely those that are left, namely to the people of God. Whence: “If they shall enter into my rest,” which in Hebrew is called the sabbath. He sanctifies these who does not carry the burden of sin on the sabbath, nor says: “as a heavy burden are become heavy upon me.” Such a one also does not gather sticks on the sabbath, nor builds upon the foundation of Christ wood, hay, stubble, nor kindles a fire to consume useless matter; and on the sabbath day he abides in one place, nor goes out abroad, but remains as a pillar set in the temple of God. Whence: “He that shall overcome, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God; and he shall go out no more.”

37_interl15928: It is not for a priest to touch a carcase, since he, who is to plead for the faults of others, ought to approach the altar clean.

37_marg4105: Except for father, etc. Rabanus. 37_marg4107: It must be known that all that the Lord here speaks through the prophet he had also foretold through Moses. Whence also the Saviour left no volume of doctrine, though the apocrypha falsely claim this, but speaks daily by the Father and his Spirit in the heart of the faithful. 37_marg4111: Great is the dignity of priests, but if they sin, the fall is grievous; let us rejoice at the ascent, but fear the fall. 37_marg4112: Allegorically. All these things are to be referred to the Church, which labours in the world and hastens to heavenly things: namely, that out of the whole world some be chosen for the possession of God, who may possess the holy place; others, who have advanced to greater things, may hold the holy of holies. Among the ministers also the order is different, namely of priests and Levites: some of whom by their prayers and virtues offer sacrifices to God daily; others, in a second and lesser rank, that they may minister to these and advance through those who have climbed to the heights of virtue. And lastly let there be a leader or prince, who may be able so far as to receive a possession against one tribe, that the merit of many may make up for the merit of each one. And first, while he lives in the world, let him possess breadth “from sea to sea.” Then from the west, or from the sea, to the east, that leaving present things behind he may hasten to the future. And let him have his own fixed possession, and let the prince not desire what belongs to others. And let each tribe hold its own part; which properly regards the apostles and priests, to whom it is said that they should not lay waste and plunder the people of God, nor possess the land of Israel by inheritance, but that each one should have his own possession, which is appointed for his rank.

37_marg4113: Anything dead of itself, etc. Rabanus. And according to the letter, to every chosen kind, royal and priestly, that is, Christian, which is anointed with spiritual oil; whence: “God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.” These precepts agree, that they not eat what is dead of itself, of birds as of cattle, whose blood has not been poured out, which in the Acts of the Apostles is called “strangled,” which the letter of the apostles from Jerusalem admonishes must necessarily be observed; and what is caught by a beast, because that too is likewise strangled. And he condemns priests who do not keep these precepts through the greed of the gullet, for thrushes, fig-peckers, dormice, and the like.
37_marg4114: Allegorically. The dead of itself is that in which the blood of the soul has died. And it imitates Nabal of Carmel, whose name means fool, who, having heard David’s anger, trembled with fear, and “his heart died within him.” But he is said to be caught by beasts (from whose bites the prophet begs not to be torn, saying: “Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee”) who is devoured by the bites of the lion, that is, the adversary; and of the leopard, who does not change his variety; and of the she-bear, which rages when her cubs are taken; and of wolves and the other beasts, which we understand in the variety of demons.
37_marg4115: And when you shall begin, etc. After the ceremonies of the priests, and their attire, and the food which they ought to take and which to avoid, he makes a description of the holy land. And before he divides it among the tribes, he commands that out of all the tribes a place be chosen which in length shall have twenty-five thousand. And because he does not add of cubits or feet or ells, it is to be understood that the reed is meant, which was in the man’s hand and had a measure of six cubits and the sixth part of one cubit, that is, the Palestinian. Let the diligent reader reckon how many reeds make a thousand paces, and how many thousands there were in length and breadth.

37_marg4117: And with this measure, etc. Rabanus. In the former temple, which is called the sanctuary, five hundred reeds are described on each side. And again five hundred cubits, by which the whole possession of the priests is separated. But in the second sanctuary, where is the holy of holies, the breadth and space of the temple are not described, but the number is uncertain; which we find also in the possession of the prince, who without any number has a possession among the people of Israel, since the progress of all overflows to the prince, and the salvation of the disciples to the teacher.
37_interl15953: as if priests will dwell in it, but only then when they perform the priestly office
37_marg4118: And five and twenty thousand, etc. Rabanus. Twenty-five refers to the five senses, which are set down four times. Ten thousand, to perfect knowledge, so that in the one case only simple history is held, and in the other there is discussion also of theology and the supernal powers. For ten is perfect. But it must be noted that the priests, who are in the higher rank, possess twenty-five thousand in length and ten in breadth. But the Levites, who are of a lower rank, have indeed the same number in length, that is, twenty-five thousand; but the breadth is limited by five. Whence also they hold only twenty store chambers, a number in which the gifts of Esau are offered. But the prince, who is truly a prince among the people and deserves to receive the name of leader, receives a possession of the sanctuary on this side and on that, that is, from all who are subject to him by their will, and is an inhabitant of the city and makes the salvation of many his reward.
37_marg4119: They will take, namely, a place for building storehouses or exedrae, according to Aquila. Chambers according to Symmachus. According to Theodotion or the Seventy, a city. Whence we understand that a certain separate place for the dwelling of the Levites is called by the name of a city.
